items.body_text:
La primera misión de Haakon como rey de Noruega tras la muerte de Harald V
El nuevo soberano afronta su primera agenda de Estado al lado de su hija, la Princesa Ingrid Alexandra
Gabriel Samaniego
Tras el fallecimiento del Rey Harald V, el deber institucional de la Casa real de Noruega esta en manos de su sucesor: Haakon VIII. El nuevo monarca inicia hoy sábado 29 de agosto su primera agenda de compromisos. Un debut en el que su ... primogénita, la princesa Ingrid Alexandra (futura heredera del trono) estará a su lado.
La primera cita oficial del rey tiene lugar en la tarde de este sábado a las 17:30 horas en el Palacio Real. Allí, el monarca y la Princesa Ingrid Alexandra recibirán en audiencia de condolencia al presidente del Storting, Masud Gharahkhani, a la presidenta del Tribunal Supremo, Toril Marie Øie, y al máximo representante de la Iglesia de Noruega, el obispo Olav Fykse Tveit. Según los medios locales, hay una gran expectación de que el soberano pueda dirigir sus primeras palabras a la nación en las próximas horas para ofrecer consuelo y marcar el inicio de esta nueva etapa.
En cuanto al funeral del Harald V, todavía no se ha fijado una fecha concreta, pero el país se encuentra oficialmente en estado de luto y algunas personas han decidido posponer celebraciones como bodas y bautizos hasta que finalice el período de duelo, según fuentes de 'NRK'.
Noticia relacionada
El próximo martes, el Rey Haakon VIII también acudirá al parlamento para pronunciar el histórico juramento prescrito por la Constitución: «Prometo y juro que gobernaré el Reino de Noruega de conformidad con su Constitución y sus leyes, ¡con la ayuda de Dios todopoderoso y omnisciente!».
La Princesa Ingrid Alexandra
Antes de matricularse en la universidad, Ingrid realizó el entrenamiento militar en el Batallón de Ingenieros de la Brigada Norte. Creció rodeada de miembros de casas reales, concretamente de sus padrinos: el rey Felipe de España y el rey Federico de Dinamarca; y de su madrina, la princesa heredera Victoria de Suecia. Al igual que su padre, la Princesa Ingrid asistió a una escuela primaria pública antes de cursar estudios en la Oslo International School, un centro privado de habla inglesa.
Ahora la joven se convierte en la primera heredera de mayoría de edad en ocupar el primer puesto de la línea de sucesión desde el inicio del reinado y, también, en la primera mujer que tendría acceso al trono de noruega en 600 años; la última monarca mujer fue la reina Margarita, fallecida en 1412. En la nueva condición de Ingrid, no solo acompañará a su padre en los actos de Estado, sino que también podrá actuar como regente en caso de ausencia o enfermedad del monarca.

items.body_text:
Fútbol
A qué hora se juega el Sevilla - Atlético de Madrid y dónde ver en televisión y online el partido de LaLiga hoy
Conoce a qué hora empieza el partido entre el Sevilla y el Atlético y dónde ver en televisión y online el encuentro de hoy, 29 de agosto
Miguel Ángel Sánchez-Flor
Madrid
La jornada tres de la Liga es la primera en la que todos los partidos se jugarán en un mismo espacio. De viernes a lunes y a la espera de recuperar los horarios habituales de la temporada. De los tres encuentros que se disputan el sábado, el encargado de cerrar este día será el enfrentamiento entre el Sevilla y el Atlético.
El Sánchez-Pizjuán acoge este duelo en el que su equipo llega con pleno de puntos. Ha salido victorioso en las dos primeras fechas. En la primera, estrenó el presente curso con una remontada al Rayo Vallecano a domicilio. Este triunfo se decidió en los últimos minutos gracias a un penalti transformado por Peque que indignó a propios y extraños.
El conjunto madrileño también se quejó de otra acción en la que se les anuló un gol por una supuesta falta de Isi. En San Mamés también se llevaron los tres puntos, esta vez con gran solvencia, pero no exentos de polémica. Yuri se marchó expulsado cuando todavía no se había abierto el marcador.
Noticia relacionada
Los rojiblancos acumulan una victoria y un empate en el inicio de campaña. Los colchoneros lograron imponerse al Málaga en el primer encuentro ante su público. El otro choque también tuvo lugar en su feudo. Comenzaron ganando al Villarreal, fueron remontados y finalmente consiguieron rascar un punto. Pero este pinchazo no fue la única nota negativa del día. Julián Álvarez se encontró por primera vez con los atléticos, tras haber hecho público su deseo de abandonar el equipo.
El argentino entró en la convocatoria, pero no partió de inicio. Cara seria en todo momento. Cuando fue nombrado por la megafonía del estadio en la previa del encuentro, recibió la primera pitada. Un rechazo que volvió a constatarse una vez saltó a calentar. Ingresó en el terreno de juego y más de lo mismo. Se sumaban algunos cánticos en su contra. El lío llegó cuando finalizó el duelo y el jugador se marchó directamente al vestuario. Separado de sus compañeros. Desde el Atlético sostienen que no fue decisión de él, sino de la entidad. Se busca proteger a un jugador que no quiere estar allí y que se encuentra en una situación de difícil solución.
A qué hora es el Sevilla - Atlético de liga hoy
El Sevilla - Atlético de Madrid, encuentro que se disputa este sábado 29 de agosto en el estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán correspondiente a la jornada 3 de LaLiga, está programado para las 21.30 horas.
Dónde ver el Sevilla - Atlético en televisión y online hoy
El encuentro entre Sevilla y Atlético de Madrid se puede ver en directo en televisión en España por M+ LALIGA (dial 54 de Movistar Plus+ y 110 de Orange TV), M+ LALIGA HDR y LALIGA TV BAR.
Los aficionados también podrán seguir el minuto a minuto del encuentro a través de la web de ABC.es, donde los lectores podrán encontrar al término del partido la crónica más completa.

items.title: The California ranch owned by the new CJNG leader, which the Trump administration is seeking to seize
items.summary: Juan Carlos Valencia González, who took control of the cartel after El Mencho’s death, owns an estate in Hemet valued at nearly $700,000
items.body_text:
The California ranch owned by the new CJNG leader, which the Trump administration is seeking to seize
Juan Carlos Valencia González, who took control of the cartel after El Mencho’s death, owns an estate in Hemet valued at nearly $700,000
He used only his mother’s surname — González — when he bought a ranch in California that was offered to him for $250,000. It was an investment Juan Carlos Valencia González made in 2011, when he was 26, without anticipating that the property’s value would nearly triple because of the U.S. state’s fast-rising real estate market. He also did not imagine he would end up leading the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), which at the time had just been founded by his stepfather, Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, “El Mencho.” That was a bet Rodríguez, also known as “El R3” or “El Pelón,” made 15 years before he became one of the world’s most-wanted drug traffickers.
The property Valencia González left behind when he went fully into crime is in Hemet, around 90 miles east of Los Angeles. It sits in a ranch community amid lots where horses graze, vacant plots, farmland, and upscale homes. Rocky, steep hills frame the pastoral landscape in the distance, far from the bustle of the United States’ second-largest metropolis. The air is clean there, although occasional gusts carry the smell of manure. This was El R3’s refuge whenever he wanted to get away from the streets of Santa Ana, the city where he was born in 1984 and where several of his relatives still live.
“Keep the gate closed. Don’t trust what the horses tell you,” “Beware of dogs” and “Security cameras and audio recorder in use,” warn the signs hung on the chain-link fence surrounding the ranch. Inside are two roosters, two dogs, a goat, and a sheep. A small, nearly dilapidated house, a wooden shed, an old, dust-covered pickup truck, and an American flag flying in the center are other signs that someone lives here.
For several years the U.S. government has had Valencia González’s ranch in its sights. The property is currently managed by the capo’s maternal uncle, José María González Valencia, who lives in Orange County, a source at the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) told EL PAÍS on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press about the matter.
At the end of July, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a federal civil forfeiture action in the District of Columbia, alleging the property is connected to the newly anointed leader of the cartel. The case, now before a judge in Washington, D.C., is being led by the Money Laundering, Narcotics, and Forfeiture Section, a unit of the DOJ Criminal Division.
The rise of El Mencho’s stepson
Valencia González is the son of Rosalinda González Valencia and Armando Valencia Cornelio, who went from being an avocado grower to one of the founders of the Milenio Cartel, a predecessor of the CJNG. That relationship was short-lived. Soon after, Rosalinda became the partner of El Mencho, with whom she had three children: Jessica Johanna, Rubén, and Laisha Michelle Oseguera González, all born in San Francisco, California. Several of Rosalinda’s brothers are also involved in the drug trade. Known as “Los Cuinis,” authorities have identified them as the CJNG’s financial arm.
That family network propelled El R3 into the CJNG’s top ranks, where he led the Grupo Elite, a hit-squad tasked primarily with protecting the cartel boss. The stepchild of El Mencho “organized numerous violent acts... in addition to manufacturing, transporting, and distributing tons of narcotics,” according to a statement from the Department of Justice, which in 2020 charged him with drug importation and firearms offenses.

items.title: Six months without El Mencho in Mexico
items.summary: The death of the CJNG leader inaugurated the state’s offensive against the criminal group that operated for years with relative impunity. The subsequent capture of major capos fuels doubts about its reorganization
items.body_text:
Six months without El Mencho in Mexico
The death of the CJNG leader inaugurated the state’s offensive against the criminal group that operated for years with relative impunity. The subsequent capture of major capos fuels doubts about its reorganization
Mexico is becoming accustomed to life without El Mencho, a towering figure in the continent’s criminal narrative who evaded justice for years while building his formidable criminal empire. Killed in a military operation six months ago in Jalisco, his absence is for now being filled by an insistent state offensive against his group, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), which he founded 15 years ago and led until his death. His downfall, the subsequent arrests of key figures in the criminal network, and the apparent pressure by authorities on others shape the present. Now the question is how the criminal structure will reorganize and what the consequences will be.
It still feels strange to imagine Mexico’s criminal landscape without El Mencho — a sensation similar to the one left by the arrest of the Sinaloa Cartel boss, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, betrayed by his longtime associates two years ago; and similar, too, to Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán’s final transfer to the United States after spectacular escapes and evasions that confounded authorities for a long time. El Mencho’s fall — in an operation that left dozens dead, among them authorities and civilians, and which turned the country’s center upside down that fateful February 22, with narco-blockades his group organized in several states — opened a new era in Mexico, whose broad outlines remain hard to discern.
The absence of the CJNG boss invites a look back at his origins, an exercise that immediately draws parallels with other criminal networks, mainly on the Pacific coast, and sketches a picture of the pioneers of trafficking in Mexico — figures who seem alien from today’s perspective. Rubén Oseguera — who later took the name Nemesio — was born in 1966 in Naranjo de Chila, a hamlet in Aguililla, a cursed town between the Tierra Caliente of Michoacán and the Sierra Costa region. Cursed, because progress — which had begun to take hold in the region with the harnessing of a couple of rivers, the Balsas and the Tepalcapetepc, for agroindustrial use, and the construction of a port on the coast in Lázaro Cárdenas — passed the town by. The logic of subsistence prevailed in the municipality. The hope for a better life seemed out of reach.
What happened, however, is that several families from Aguililla rebelled. They gambled on a singular business: growing marijuana for export. Historian Enrique Guerra Manzo of the National Autonomous University of Mexico explains that “as early as the 1930s and 1940s there were narcotics crops in Aguililla, but they became widespread in the postwar period.” Marijuana gave way to poppy, the raw material for heroin. The hesitations of the early years led to an industry that by the late 1960s looked robust. When El Mencho was born, California hippies were consuming increasing amounts of cannabis from Mexico. San Francisco’s Summer of Love led the farmers of the canyons in southwest Michoacán to prosper.
The main family in marijuana and poppy cultivation in the area were the Valencias. “The Valencias are from Dos Aguas, a hamlet of Aguililla, and the family patriarch is credited with introducing poppy to Michoacán,” Guerra says, referring to Miguel Ángel Félix Cornejo, who was murdered in 1994. “In those times, in the 1970s and 1980s, everyone knew each other around there. Dos Aguas, Naranjo de Chila, El Aguaje, El Limón form a tightly linked triangle. That’s where the Valencias and El Mencho come from,” Guerra explains; he is the author of a monumental study on crime in the area, Territorios violentos en México. El caso de Tierra Caliente, Michoacán (Violent Regions in Mexico: The Case of Tierra Caliente, Michoacán, 2022).

items.title: Marcelo Lucero’s killing returns to the spotlight 18 years later: ‘The violence is back, but now it comes from ICE agents’
items.summary: A petition before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights argues that the US government bears part of the responsibility for the murder of the Ecuadorian migrant on Long Island by failing to curb hateful rhetoric against Latinos
items.body_text:
Marcelo Lucero’s killing returns to the spotlight 18 years later: ‘The violence is back, but now it comes from ICE agents’
A petition before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights argues that the US government bears part of the responsibility for the murder of the Ecuadorian migrant on Long Island by failing to curb hateful rhetoric against Latinos
He wears a light pink dress shirt and a blue suit. It’s an important day.
At 4 p.m., in Washington, D.C., Joselo Lucero takes his seat. He’s in a building that’s located on F Street Northwest. In the room, sitting around him, there are lawyers, the staff of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the president of the LatinoJustice organization, representatives of the U.S. government, along with other attendees of the public hearing being held by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR).
Among all those present, Joselo Lucero is the only one who will break down in tears.
He has waited for this moment for almost two decades, ever since his brother, Marcelo Lucero, was the victim of a hate crime that set off alarm bells on Long Island and throughout New York. The murder occurred 18 years ago, but no one can assure Joselo that it could not have happened yesterday, today or next week.
Joselo takes the floor: “No immigrant family should ever have to go through something like this: learning that my brother was killed because he looked like me. I’m a citizen of this country, but I don’t feel safe, not in 2008 and not in 2026.”
The chair of the commission announces Oswaldo Marcelo Lucero et al. v. United States, Case No. 13.735, which is the first of its kind to come before the IACHR. It is seeking to have the U.S. government acknowledge its responsibility in the death of an Ecuadorian migrant on November 8, 2008. That was when Manuel Lucero was killed by a group of seven teenagers, who called themselves the “Caucasian Crew.” The argument is that there was a systemic failure behind the killing of a single individual: authorities had never meaningfully confronted the anti-Latino hate rhetoric that helped make such violence possible.
Joselo takes the microphone. He’s asked not to speak for too long, but to explain, for all those following the case, who his brother was, what happened that fateful night and what impact his death has had on the entire family.
Joselo begins reliving, as he has done so many times over the years, the moment he learned that his 37-year-old brother, the eldest of Doña Rosario’s four children, would no longer be there to share dinner with the family or call from his nearby home on Long Island, in Suffolk County, to check in on him or ask when he would be coming home. Marcelo, he says, was a “very strict” older brother.
Doña Rosario raised her children largely on her own in Gualaceo, about 21 miles east of Cuenca, Ecuador, after their father died when they were still young. She made food to sell, and her children helped her. “She taught us the values of hard work and respect for others. But also the value of education,” Joselo says.
Marcelo was the first of the siblings to leave Gualaceo. Back in 1993, he traveled as far as New York City. He was 24 years old. “My brother’s decision to come to the United States is the same one made by many young people in our countries: he wanted to a better life and to help his family.” Joselo followed him almost two years later. He had just turned 20.
At the time, there was no sign of what lay ahead, that he would one day become the person desperately seeking justice for his murdered brother.
On Sunday, November 9, 2008, Joselo was at home when a detective from Long Island knocked on the door. At first, he didn’t answer.

items.title: The Hague Mayor orders activists to stop the A12 blockade; 2 arrested so far
items.summary: The Hague Mayor Jan van Zanen ordered the Extinction Rebellion to immediately clear the A12, or they will be removed.
items.body_text:
The Hague Mayor orders activists to stop the A12 blockade; 2 arrested so far
Updated at 14:20 to mention the two arrests.
The Hague Mayor Jan van Zanen ordered the Extinction Rebellion to immediately clear the A12, or they will be removed. The activists walked out on the Utrechtsebaan from off-ramps at around 1 p.m., creating a traffic jam of people wanting to leave the city.
Two protestors have already been arrested for refusing to leave. According to the ANP, the arrests happened just before the police told the activists to clear the road.
A spokesperson for XR told NOS that it is "not forbidden" to protest on the highway. "If we are charged for blocking the highway, then of course we will challenge that in court.” The XR has previously staged multiple blockades on the highway.
Earlier this week, mayors, the Public Prosecution Service, the police, and Minister of Justice Van Weel said in a statement that there will be criminal action against any highway blockades.
"Demonstrating is a fundamental right, and we protect that. But expressing your opinion is different from making the highway or railway unsafe," the joint statement read. "Our main message is to prevent dangerous situations caused by slow movements and to not block highways. That puts others in danger, and we do not accept that."
On August 14 on the A59 near Heesch, two people died and six others were injured in an accident at the end of a traffic jam caused by farmers driving tractors on the highway.
Reporting by ANP and NL Times

items.title: Belgian authorities investigate whether Dutch mass sperm donor fathered local children
items.summary: Belgian authorities are looking into whether Simon, the newly discovered Dutch mass
items.body_text:
Belgian authorities investigate whether Dutch mass sperm donor fathered local children
Belgian authorities are looking into whether Simon, the newly discovered Dutch mass donor, also donated sperm in Belgium through fertility clinics or informal channels.
Simon, who also went by Daan, Saam, Jesse, Johan, and Maarten, is from the Groningen region and is believed to have fathered at least 120 children in the Netherlands. Dutch media now also suggests that he might have also donated sperm in the neighboring country.
Nieuwsuur, which was the first to report on Simon, also reported that he might have children in countries including Denmark and Germany. One of the mothers found other kids in Germany by using an online DNA database.
The investigation is being conducted by the Belgian Federal Agency for Medicines and Health Products (FAMHP). Mass sperm donation, especially within the same country, raises the chances of children later unknowingly entering incestuous relationships.
In the Netherlands, Simon reportedly spent around 15 years actively donating sperm. He had also reportedly lied to the future mothers about the number of kids he’s already fathered. He is believed to have mostly reached out to the women directly with offers through different online platforms.
The Donor Child Foundation told ANP it is in contact with a group of mothers in the Netherlands who have the donors’ children.
Simon was previously in contact with Nieuwsuur when they interviewed him for another story, not knowing that he was also a mass donor. When contacted recently about this case, he declined to comment. "I consciously choose to conduct any potential contact exclusively anonymously with the mothers themselves or through the official authority," he told the program.
Reporting by ANP and NL Times

items.body_text:
Consumer watchdog issues warning after rat feces found in Eindhoven care home kitchen
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) gave an official warning to the care institution Vitalis after rat feces were found in the kitchen of the Kronehoef care home in Eindhoven.
The residents of the building have been struggling with a rat infestation for a while, according to Omroep Brabant. NVWA inspectors arrived after multiple reports of possessions being chewed on by rats and the rodents’ feces and urine everywhere.
An 82-year-old woman was also bitten by a rat. She had previously found rat droppings all over her room, including inside the bed. “She didn't want to call the nurses because she knew they are afraid of vermin,” the woman’s daughter told the newspaper. "The Vitalis staff no longer dared to go inside. I had to feed her, shower her, and dress her myself.”
Rat exterminators had been previously called in, and traps were set up, but little reportedly changed.
"We only supervise places where food is stored and prepared, so the kitchens," a spokesperson for the NVWA said on Friday. "There were feces lying in a few hard-to-reach places."
The building itself is owned by the housing corporation Wooninc. The organization said it is "doing everything together with Vitalis to resolve the nuisance as quickly as possible."
Reports of rat-related problems have been rising all over the Netherlands, and drought might be the reason, according to the Knowledge and Advisory Center for Animal Pests.

items.body_text:
Dutch men out of hockey World Cup as women prepare for final
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch men’s hockey team have missed out on a home World Cup final, losing their semi-final to Spain in Amstelveen on Friday, the day before the Dutch women play for the title.
Spain, coached by the former Netherlands manager Max Caldas, won 4-3 at the Wagener Stadium.
The game turned in the final quarter, with the score at 1-1, when striker Duco Telgenkamp was sent to the sin bin for 10 minutes for pushing a Spanish defender to the ground.
With Telgenkamp off the pitch, Spain scored three times to go 4-1 ahead, José Basterra completing a hat-trick. Jip Janssen and Joep de Mol pulled two goals back late on, but Spain held the lead.
The result ended the Dutch men’s hopes of a first world title since 1998. They will play Argentina for bronze on Sunday in Wavre, Belgium, where Spain will meet defending champions Germany in the final.
The Dutch women, meanwhile, reached the final with a 1-0 win over Belgium and will face Argentina at the Wagener Stadium at 4pm on Saturday. Victory would give them a fourth successive world title, a feat no country has achieved.

items.summary: Our regular columnist Molly Quell drove through Belgium and France on her holiday and has developed some strong feelings about...
items.body_text:
Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Our regular columnist Molly Quell drove through Belgium and France on her holiday and has developed some strong feelings about road design.
I’ve just returned from the most sacred of Dutch annual traditions. No, not early Sinterklaas festivities or a kring party for my mother-in-law’s birthday.
The yearly pilgrimage to France.
Don’t tell the authorities, as they may well take my passport, but this was my first year making the summer trek south to soak up the sun, drink plenty of wine and contribute to the wear and tear on Belgian roads.
In fact, as a childless adult, I don’t often take a proper summer holiday. Who wants to pay three times more to have your vacation infested with irritable parents and their inevitably sticky children?
I usually have my vacation during the school year when the temperatures are better and teenagers are locked up in educational institutions rather than blasting an unending roll of TikToks at full volume at the table next to mine while their parents order more drinks and pretend everyone is enjoying the perfect summer getaway.
But due to a series of unfortunate events, (namely, being at the mercy of the schedules of people who do have children) I took part in the annual ritual of packing up a car and driving many, many hours to spend time complaining about the French in France.
As I rarely have the opportunity to drive around rural Belgium and France, my husband and I decided to make the most of it and tick off a series of “places we’d like to see but aren’t worth planning an entire weekend around.”
Dunkirk. Omaha Beach. Jules Verne’s grave (very cool). Jardins d’Étretat (also cool). Mont-Saint-Michel (less cool and more like the temperature of Satan’s sauna in August).
We saw a lot of things and thus we did a lot of driving. Therefore, I now consider myself an expert on the ins and outs of Western European roadway infrastructure.
It is classist and problematic to mock the Belgians for their accents. It is simply stating objective and true facts when you mock their roads. It isn’t merely the quality of the roads (which can have a sort of deep tissue massage effect) that is bad but how they are designed.
It is as though Belgian road engineers are required to sample every single variety of local Trappist beer before planning an interchange.
Belgian drivers are also unhinged, but in fairness if I had to commute over Mad Max-style infrastructure every day, I would also operate a motor vehicle like I had no regard for human life.
The French are much better drivers. There is plenty to disparage about the French as a nation and a people, but the overall quality of their driving is very good. They do have the tendency to drive a bit close to the bumper, which my Dutch husband suggests they could improve by “having more than six minutes of driving lessons.”
What is confusing about French roads is the liberal use of the term “round about” for any jumble of intersecting roads without a stop light. Roundabouts have a shape. It’s literally in the name. French roundabouts are what happens when the children of drunk Belgian road engineers scribble on the design plans.
At least the French are largely forgiving of cars with foreign plates driving through their convoluted roundabouts Mario Kart style.
Given these experiences, you would think returning back over the border at the end of the journey would be a welcome relief. It was certainly a relief for my jaw, which I no longer had to clench to keep my molars from bashing together, but the Dutch are not without their own problems.
South of the border, there was a general regard for the speed limit. The occasional outlier (nearly always in a BMW) would fly past you in Belgium or France, but mostly people minded the rules.

items.title: Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo
items.summary: A member of the executive on Oldebroek council in Gelderland has apologised for posting a photograph of himself posing with...
items.body_text:
Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A member of the executive on Oldebroek council in Gelderland has apologised for posting a photograph of himself posing with a Kalashnikov in front of a pro-Russian flag. Standing next to him in the photo is a former Almere council candidate for the far-right FvD party, according to the Volkskrant.
Tom de Nooijer, of the local Christelijk Verbond Oldebroek party, shared the image on Instagram after visiting Transnistria, a self-declared, unrecognised pro-Russian region that broke away from Moldova after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
De Nooijer said he had been on holiday in Moldova and travelled to the region out of a “historical interest in the Soviet past”, and went to a shooting range there. He said the trip was private and not meant as a political statement. He is a former presenter of the right-wing broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland.
He initially declined to comment or apologise, prompting anger from opposition councillors. “They fled the violence he is glorifying by posing for a pro-Russian flag,” said Frank van ’t Ende, referring to the 200 Ukrainian refugees the council houses. A ChristenUnie councillor called the photo “shocking”.
Mayor Tanja Haseloop-Amsing told Omroep Gelderland that the council’s executive had been “unpleasantly surprised” by the image.
In a written statement on Wednesday, De Nooijer distanced himself from the hammer-and-sickle flag in the photo, called the visit unwise and apologised to anyone who might have been insulted.

items.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
items.summary: Daniel Tilles Politicians should let Poland’s achievements speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
By Daniel Tilles
Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story.
Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland.
“A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries.
Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising.
Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table.
Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years.
In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025
Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown.
In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States.
However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative.
The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations.
Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US.
The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026
The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”.
The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead.
The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eis

Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing.
The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024.
Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok.
Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków
🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns
— Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026
The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year.
Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year.
Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty.
The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point.
Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level.
Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year.
Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates.
Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising.
What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025
The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules.
In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028.
However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record.
“The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.”

items.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
items.summary: The remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead.
The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger.
In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine.
The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered.
Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.
The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later.
“It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN.
The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning.
“In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living.
However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element.
Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin.
“The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska.
The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland
Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023

items.title: Starlink 'trains' spotted over Estonia, mistaken for UFOs
items.summary: "UFOs" or "shooting stars" recently reported spotted in Estonia's night sky are in fact Starlink satellite trains, Tartu Postimees said.
items.body_text:
Starlink 'trains' spotted over Estonia, mistaken for UFOs
"UFOs" or "shooting stars" recently reported spotted in Estonia's night sky are in fact Starlink satellite trains, Tartu Postimees said.
The satellites are new additions to SpaceX's Starlink network, which aims to provide high‑speed internet access globally, and brings nearly 10,000 satellites in low orbit and new launches taking place at least twice a week the paper reporetd.
After launch, the satellites remain closely grouped in a line, as the name suggests, but once they reach their operational altitude, they disperse and become ordinary faint points of light.
Enthusiasts can track when the next "string of pearls" will be visible over their location using apps like Satellite Tracker.
There are nearly 10,000 satellites in relatively low orbit (300–500 kilometers altitude), the paper said, plus GPS and other satellites which orbit much further from the earth.
The Elon Musk-founded SpaceX's Starlink is a satellite‑based internet service designed to bring connectivity to remote areas, crisis zones and places where cable internet does not reach, using a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit.
--

Editor: Andrew Whyte

items.title: Ancient Bonfires organizer: Three fires registered in America this year
items.summary: Mairold Vaik, organizer of the Night of Ancient Bonfires, told Vikerraadio that, interestingly, it has rained on the event only twice in the past 18 years.
items.body_text:
Ancient Bonfires organizer: Three fires registered in America this year
Mairold Vaik, organizer of the Night of Ancient Bonfires, told Vikerraadio that, interestingly, it has rained on the event only twice in the past 18 years.
"The Night of Ancient Bonfires tradition began in the early 1990s when two friends — one on the Tahkuna Peninsula on Hiiumaa and the other near Turku in Finland — agreed to light bonfires together and send good thoughts to each other across the sea," Mairold Vaik explained. He added that when he learned about the tradition a few years later, he was particularly drawn to the sense of unity it created. "That feeling is what keeps me taking part in the tradition."
Vaik, who compiles information about different bonfires on a shared map on the Night of Ancient Bonfires website, said he began collecting reports of bonfires from people he knew in 2009. "At first it was a simple Google Maps map, but for years now there has been a separate website."
"When I look at the list right now, there aren't that many bonfires listed. There are around 50 public bonfires and another 45 to 50 private ones, so a little over 100 in total. But what I can say is that the map isn't as popular anymore as the event itself," he stressed, adding that there are probably 10 times as many bonfires as are shown on the map.
"We've even received three bonfire reports from the United States. Estonians there have also gotten together and will be enjoying the evening. We've also received some reports from around the Baltic Sea — from Latvia, Sweden and Finland — and there's even one from the eastern shore of the Gulf of Finland."
According to Vaik, no one dictates how the Night of Ancient Bonfires should be celebrated. "No one tells you the right way to celebrate Midsummer Day either. But from my own experience, I can say that the best bonfire site is your own, with a small group of your own people."
"Bonfire events haven't been canceled because of rain, but it really is remarkable that, by my estimate, on the evening when the bonfires are lit, rain has fallen in parts of Estonia only twice in the past 18 years," he said, adding that there could be a brief shower on the islands of western Estonia during this year's Night of Ancient Bonfires. "Fortunately, no rain is forecast for mainland Estonia."
The fires are lit on the last Saturday of August, which this year is August 29, at sunset.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Kaspar Viilup

items.title: Gallery: Siim Kallas sent off with state honors
items.summary: Former Prime Minister Siim Kallas will be laid to rest with state honors on Saturday.
items.body_text:
Gallery: Siim Kallas sent off with state honors
Former Prime Minister Siim Kallas will be laid to rest with state honors on Saturday.
The hearse began its journey in Viimsi, from where traveled through Tallinn and via Toompea to the Estonia Concert Hall.
The first memorial stop was at the Viimsi municipal government building where representatives of the Viimsi municipal government and council had gathered. Siim Kallas lived in Viimsi and served as mayor of Viimsi Municipality from 2017 to 2019.
In Tallinn, the hearse stopped outside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bank of Estonia, Ministry of Finance, Riigikogu and Stenbock House.
The hearse then arrived at the Estonia Concert Hall. The coffin was received with military honors by the Guard Battalion's honor guard and the military band of the Estonian Defense Forces.
Inside the Estonia Concert Hall, representatives of Viimsi Municipality, the Reform Party, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Finance, Bank of Estonia and Riigikogu stood guard of honor beside the coffin.
President Alar Karis said in a speech at Siim Kallas' memorial ceremony that Kallas was never afraid of bold ideas for advancing life in Estonia and knew that ideas also had to be put into practice, because otherwise there was a risk of remaining invisible in a small and distant corner of the world.
"That is precisely how he helped Estonia grow into a modern country that values freedom and did everything in his power to bring us back into Europe," Karis said.
Following Karis' remarks, the current and former prime ministers placed a parliamentary gavel on the coffin.
Prime Minister and Reform Party Chair Kristen Michal said in his eulogy that the measure of a statesman lies not only in making decisions at the right time, but also in those decisions proving to be right decades later. "Siim Kallas had that fortunate touch, coupled with a sharp mind, courage and perseverance!"
Siim Kallas died on August 22 at the age of 77. He served as Estonia's prime minister, foreign minister and finance minister, governor of the Bank of Estonia, vice president of the European Commission and a member of the Riigikogu on several occasions. Kallas was one of the authors of the Self-Managing Estonia (IME) proposal, one of the leaders of the 1992 monetary reform and one of the founders of the Reform Party.
--
Editor: Mirjam Mäekivi, Marcus Turovski

items.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
items.summary: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague was guilty of "uncivilised" and "unjustifiable" behaviour for not releasing the Bosnian Serb genocide convict before his death this week.
items.body_text:
Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.
“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.
He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.
On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.
Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.
“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.
“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.
Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.
Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.
However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

items.title: Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
items.summary: President Jakov Milatovic has called an emergency session of the country’s Defence and Security Council after claims that two neighbour states are seeking to destabilise Montenegro and obstruct its EU accession progress.
items.body_text:
Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
President Jakov Milatovic’s office said on Friday that he has called the heads of the country’s security sector Defence and Security Council after allegations by Prime Minister Milojko Spajic that the country faces “hybrid threats” from two of its neighbours.
Spajic claimed that officials from at least two countries in the region are involved in coordinated activity aimed at destabilising Montenegro and undermining its path towards European Union membership.
Milatovic’s office said the security chiefs will be asked to provide precise information on Spajic’s allegations, as well as a comprehensive assessment of the country’s security situation.
Spajic said on Thursday that Montenegro had “serious operational security information” that threats would accompany the country’s expected progress in opening new EU negotiating chapters. Montenegro is currently seen as the frontrunner among Balkan states to become the next EU member.
“According to our information, such activities are aimed at destabilising Montenegro, with the expected support of certain political actors and part of the media scene in our country,” Spajic posted on X.
On Friday, Montenegrin newspaper Vijesti reported that Serbia and Albania are the two countries referred to by Spajic.
Vijesti quoted an unnamed source who said that some key players in the region were unhappy with Montenegro’s rapid progress toward European integration and wanted to slow it down.
Another anonymous source quoted by the newspaper claimed that a senior government official was vulnerable because of compromising information that could be used by foreign powers. The source suggested that the official’s political party might leave the ruling coalition as a result.
Milatovic’s office said that the president was concerned by the reports, and that “the public has the right to know which official this is”. But it added that serious security issues should not be used to score political points.
“Issues concerning the security and stability of the state must be addressed responsibly, based on facts and through the institutions of the system,” it said.
The warning did not stop some prominent figures connecting the security issue to responses to the death on Thursday of the Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic.
After parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic stated that he had sent condolences to the former general’s family, the head of Montenegro’s Islamic Community, Rifat Fejzic, asked if politicians who “mourn war criminals [are] in collusion with this hybrid war?”
Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha has rejected the suggestion that his country was part of any “destabilising scenario” in Montenegro. Posting on X, Hoxha insisted that the allegations could not “artificially create problems between our two countries”.
“Although no formal accusations have been articulated against Albania, I wish to state clearly and strongly that Albania is not, and cannot be, part of any destabilising scenario, whether in Montenegro – a neighbour, friend, partner, and NATO ally with whom we share the same EU membership goal – or anywhere else,” he wrote.

items.title: Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
items.summary: From Turkey’s search for peace to Serbia’s creeping elections, our selection of Premium stories takes a look at the hopes and dilemmas bubbling away in the background of these developments.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
Forcing a deal
The question of who owns Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state property is a major point of dispute and an unresolved issue on the country’s path away from supervision by the Office of the High Representative and towards membership of the EU. Not surprising, perhaps, in a country where the core issue of sovereignty is contested.
Intractable though the issue may seem, might there be movement towards resolving it? Washington’s newly-discovered interest in energy, mining and infrastructure projects in the country is putting the spotlight on this issue. Now the question is whether Bosnia will solve the issue of state property on Washington’s terms or its own.
Read more: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property? (August 21, 2026)
Pre-campaigning
Will he? Won’t he? For much of the year, Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic has kept the public guessing over if and when he might call early elections. Indeed, Vucic himself may still not have made up his mind.
But in the meantime, the Serbian leader has been on a blitz tour of the country, visiting factories, checking on roadworks and hearing the pleas and grievances of ordinary people. The pace and scale of the campaign have caught many by surprise. In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Bojan Vranic dissects the motivation for Vucic’s manoeuvres.
Read more: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout (August 24, 2026)
Courting Trump
As the conflict between the US and Iran limps on, ordinary Americans are feeling the pinch. So, it seems, are Donald Trump’s approval ratings on handling the economy, as November’s crucial mid-term elections approach.
Yet while Trump’s appeal may be tanking in the US, his star still shines in faraway corners of the world, including the Balkans. In her regular ‘Letter from Washington’ column, Jovana Djurovic takes a look at the latest attempts by Balkan countries and their leaders to ingratiate themselves with Trump.
Read more: Letter from Washington: Buying Trump’s Favour with UFC in Serbia, Arms in Albania (August 27, 2026)
Making peace
As Turkey moves to end its four decade-long conflict with the Kurdish PKK militant group, the prospect of peace is opening up new dilemmas for Kurdish villagers displaced by years of fighting. Tens of thousands of people have fled areas of fighting over the decades, leaving several thousand villages depopulated.
With peace apparently within grasp, some of those displaced are revisiting their homes and villages. While many long to return for good, rebuilding normal life in most of these villages will be anything but simple, as our report shows.
Read more: As Turkey Makes Peace, Kurdish Villagers Who Fled Conflict Contemplate Return (August 25, 2026)
Brewing resistance
Have people across the Balkans had enough of foreign-backed luxury development projects? Campaigns against two very prominent projects linked to the Trump family in Serbia and Albania seem to suggest so.
In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Ted Todorovic-Thomas takes a look at whether something is stirring across the region. He argues that the trend has deeper and more long-standing roots.
Read more: Across the Balkans, Foreign-Backed Luxury Developments Cause Local Anger (August 25, 2026)
Missing millions
In 2017, a private company agreed a concession with the Albanian government to build and operate a waste disposal and incineration facility outside the capital, Tirana. By 2023, some 104 million euros had been transferred to the company in public funds and other revenues.
But there was a catch. When the state took over the project in 2023, there was next to nothing to show for all the money spent. Our investigation takes a look at the ongoing trial over the missing money behind Albania’s ghost incinerators.
Read more: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators (August 21, 2026)

Between August 28 and September 12, the company is organizing tours of the floodplain forest combined with […] The post Gemenc Forests Come Alive to the Roar of the Red Deer Rut appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The event will offer a wider range of programs than a regular day at the zoo.Continue reading
The red deer rut is already in full swing, with the stags bellowing in Gemenc (southern Hungary), one of Europe’s largest contiguous floodplain forests, according to a post by Gemenc Zrt. on the Pörböly Ecotourism Center’s Facebook page. Between August 28 and September 12, the company is organizing tours of the floodplain forest combined with educational presentations, during which visitors can hear the animals’ bellowing.
The excursions depart from the Pörböly Ecotourism Center at 6:30 p.m. on August 28, 29, and September 4, 5, 11, and 12. On the deer rut listening tours, visitors can not only experience, without disturbing the wildlife, the stags’ mating calls, but also gain a better understanding of this unique phenomenon through educational, interactive presentations.
Although participation in these tours is generally not recommended for children, since the tours last several hours and are only effective if visitors listen quietly throughout,
a tour specifically for children will be organized on September 12 at one of the forest railway’s stops, Lassi, where craft activities will also be available for the little ones who quickly tire of sitting quietly and listening, organizers pointed out.
Further information about the tours and registration details can be found on the Facebook page of the Gemenc Ecotourism Center.
Via MTI; Featured photo: Pexels

The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely. François Wakenhut was responding to an open […] The post EU Acknowledges Concerns Over Asbestos Contamination appeared first o
items.body_text:
Temporary chemical measures on affected roads must not distract from the fact that the government still lacks a genuine and transparent action plan.Continue reading
The European Commission acknowledges the seriousness of concerns over asbestos contamination in Hungary, the head of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment informed Laurie Kazan-Allen, coordinator of an international organization advocating an asbestos ban. The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely.
François Wakenhut was responding to an open letter written in early July by 14 international anti-asbestos occupational safety, health, and environmental protection organizations and experts to the leaders of the European Union and Hungary.
In the document, they drew attention to the gravity of the situation in Szombathely, highlighting the dangers posed by the contamination, posing a particular threat to children’s health.
In a letter written on behalf of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the director-general emphasized that it is primarily the responsibility of the competent national authorities to ensure compliance with applicable EU rules in such cases, to assess the risks, and to take the necessary protective and remediation measures.
The European Commission is confident that the national authorities will continue to act swiftly and decisively to protect public health in the affected areas,”
François Wakenhut stated.
The asbestos contamination scandal broke out the day after Hungary’s parliamentary elections, when in Vas County the head of the environmental protection department at the local government office and the mayor of Szombathely announced at an emergency press conference that, in one of the city’s single-family residential areas, on several streets of the “Oladi Plateau,” crushed stone containing asbestos had been spread years earlier. Airborne asbestos fibers are seriously harmful to health.
István Orbán, director general of the government office, said that, according to reports, four quarries in Burgenland, Austria, had previously been closed due to high asbestos content, and they suspect the material may have come from there.
András Nemény, mayor of Szombathely, announced that 12 kilometers of streets in that part of the city are covered with asbestos-contaminated crushed stone, and the cost of safely removing and disposing of it exceeds the city’s financial resources.
To access the force majeure fund, he appealed to both the outgoing government and the incoming government for assistance. Tibor Navracsics, the outgoing Minister of Regional Development, promised to make the fund available, and a supporting government resolution was passed, but only the local government was able to take concrete steps; to prevent dust from spreading, they began regularly watering the affected streets and even applied a layer of bitumen to some sections, while awaiting guidance from experts on exactly what steps to take.
In the following weeks, several municipalities in Vas County—including Kőszeg, Lukácsháza, Bük, and Sárvár—reported that they might also be affected; laboratory tests revealed asbestos levels exceeding the threshold in all of these locations.
In Táplánszentkereszt, the areas in front of the daycare center, kindergarten, and school were inadvertently covered with asbestos-containing material; there, too, the local government had no other option but to spray the area with calcium chloride. In Bük, the local government had the material removed at its own expense, in compliance with regulations governing hazardous materials.
In Szombathely, weekly public forums were held; construction in the area was halted due to the imposed restrictions, and heavy vehicle traffic was temporarily banned and then restricted during certain periods.

I only found out on Facebook that Béla Csiszár, the representative for the Fejér 1 congressional district and also […] The post Wind Power Plans Draw Criticism as Mayors Are Sidelined appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The company aims to reduce its exposure to energy costs over the long term.Continue reading
Wind turbines are to be built in Fejér County. András Cser-Palkovics, the mayor of Székesfehérvár, stated that they were deliberately excluded from the negotiations, Világgazdaság reported.
“Is not Székesfehérvár part of the Fejér 1 congressional district? I only found out on Facebook that Béla Csiszár, the representative for the Fejér 1 congressional district and also our city’s representative, had organized an online forum on the topic of wind turbines for the (quote!) ‘mayors of the municipalities in his district.’
I do not understand why Székesfehérvár did not receive an invitation to this meeting,”
wrote András Cser-Palkovics (FIDESZ), mayor of the city with county rights, in his Facebook post on Wednesday.
“I did not think this would need to be emphasized again, but Székesfehérvár is also part of the Fejér 1 electoral district. It is the center of both the county and the electoral district. The government previously announced that it would include local municipalities in the wind power program. I would like to point out that Székesfehérvár is also a local community—one that rightfully expects answers to such a controversial issue, which also involves strategic and environmental policy matters. I would therefore have liked to participate in the consultation.
After all, local communities must not be left out of the decision-making process,”
András Cser-Palkovics added.
The mayor made it clear that they would have to take this matter into their own hands in the future. He concluded his remarks by announcing that he would provide details shortly.
On Thursday afternoon, he reported in a comment under his own post that Béla Csiszár (TISZA) had since initiated a personal meeting with him on this topic. “I certainly welcome this and am grateful for it! I believe it is important that we discuss matters affecting our city, as well as government plans, from time to time, and that we are able to inform the public about them—jointly, if necessary. I am also open to making this a regular practice,” wrote the mayor.
Via Világgazdaság; Featured photo: Pexels

items.title: Római őrhajó másolata futott zátonyra a Dráva horvát szakaszán
items.summary: A 18 méteres, fából készült hajótestet a hadsereg tolta újra vízre, majd inkább kamionra pakolták egy kikötőben.
items.body_text:
Római őrhajó másolata futott zátonyra a Dráva horvát szakaszán
Horvát katonák és tűzoltók mentették ki a Drávából egy 4. századi római őrhajó 18 méter hosszú másolatát, ami egy európai kutatási projekt keretében érkezett Horvátországba, majd Eszék közelében az alacsony vízállás miatt egy homokpadon rekedt – írta szombaton a Jutarnji List a védelmi minisztérium közleményére hivatkozva. A Danuvina Alacris nevű fahajót a sikeres művelet után pénteken visszaszállították Németországba – írja az MTI.
A német Erlangen-Nürnbergi Egyetem akkor kért segítséget a horvát hadseregtől, amikor világossá vált, hogy az apadó folyóban veszteglő hajó súlyosan megsérülhet. A mentésben 18 katona vett részt. Különleges csúszótalpakat készítettek, amikkel visszajuttatták a hajót a vízbe, majd egy vontatóhajóval Nemetin kikötőjébe vontatták.
A műveletet nehezítette, hogy a porózus faszerkezet a vízbe kerülve nagy mennyiségű vizet szívott magába. A hajó jelentősen elnehezült, és már a süllyedés veszélye is fenyegette, ezért az eszéki tűzoltók folyamatosan szivattyúzták belőle a vizet. Nemetinben végül daruval emelték közúti szállítójárműre.
A Jutarnji List szerint a mintegy öt tonnás hajót egy Németországban feltárt régészeti lelet alapján építették. Elkészítéséhez tölgyfát, mintegy négyezer szeget és római kori szerszámok másolatait használták, értékét pedig körülbelül egymillió euróra becsülik.
A Danuvina Alacris a Római Birodalom dunai határvidékén használt katonai járőrhajók működőképes rekonstrukciója. A Living Danube Limes európai projekt keretében 2020 és 2022 között készült. A kutatók nemcsak bemutatókon használják, hanem hajóznak is vele, hogy tanulmányozzák az ókori folyami közlekedést.

items.title: Trump sorozatban lőtte lábon a republikánusokat, a demokraták mégis óriásit kockáztatnak
items.summary: Végéhez közeledik az amerikai előválasztási szezon, ami demokrata oldalról a szélsőségek megerősödéséről, míg a republikánusoknál az egyre népszerűtlenebb Trump hanyatló befolyásáról szólt. Hatalmas a novemberi félidős választás tétje Trump ciklusának hátralévő két évére.
items.body_text:
Trump sorozatban lőtte lábon a republikánusokat, a demokraták mégis óriásit kockáztatnak
„Ki a pénzzel a politikából! Pénzt az emberek zsebébe! Egészségbiztosítást mindenkinek!”
Ez a szlogen volt hallható minden kampánygyűlésen, ahol Abdul El-Sayed megfordult. Az orvosból lett politikus markánsan baloldali populista arcéllel indult Michigan állam demokrata párti szenátusi előválasztásán, amit egy hajszállal ugyan, de megnyert az establishment jelöltje előtt.
Időközben ugyanabban az államban a republikánusok is előválasztást tartottak, egyebek között a csatatérkörzetnek számító nyolcas választókerület kongresszusi képviselőjelölti helyéért. Itt a Donald Trump elnök által támogatott Amir Hassan közel húsz százalékponttal kapott ki attól a Thomas Smithtől, aki hónapokkal korábban beszüntette a kampányát.
A két esemény rávilágít az amerikai előválasztási versenyek eddigi tanulságaira kicsit több mint két hónappal a félidős választás előtt.
Az egyik oldalon ott van a feltörekvő balszél, amely Izrael-ellenességgel, populista gazdasági ígéretekkel és kompromisszummentes retorikával kerekedik felül a megfáradt, erejét vesztett establishmenten. A másik oldalon pedig a pártját egy évtized óta domináló Trump igyekszik megőrizni a befolyását, miközben történelmi mélységekbe zuhanó népszerűségi mutatókkal fordul rá második elnöki ciklusa utolsó két évére. A valóság persze nem ennyire egyszerű. Több államban a progresszív baloldal jelöltje nem tudta megverni a centrista jelöltet, míg sok esetben Trump képes volt érvényesíteni akaratát, és leszámolt az ellene szegülő republikánusokkal.
Összességében azonban egy olyan kép rajzolódik ki a novemberi félidős választások előtt, amelyben az iráni háború és a gazdasági gondok miatt meggyengült republikánusokat egyetlen dolog mentheti meg a teljes kiütéstől: ha a demokraták tömegesen olyan szélsőségek felé hajló jelölteket indítanak, akik elriasztják a mérsékelt, középen álló szavazókat. Nélkülük ugyanis valószínűtlen, hogy vissza tudják szerezni a törvényhozást, amelynek jelenleg mindkét házában republikánus többség van.
Populista fordulat a demokratáknál
Az elmúlt két év meghatározó konfliktusa az amerikai politikában nem a republikánusok és a demokraták hagyományos szembenállása, hanem a Demokrata Párton belüli hatalmi átrendeződés volt. A 2010-es években már ébredező pártbeli balszél sokáig rendre alulmaradt a mérsékeltebb jelöltekkel szemben az előválasztásokon. A mérsékeltek fő ütőkártyája az volt, hogy azt állították, csak ők képesek legyőzni a végzetes fenyegetésként kezelt Trumpot és az általa vezetett MAGA-mozgalmat, a demokraták törzsszavazói pedig sokáig hittek is ebben.
Trump azonban visszatért, miután Joe Biden visszalépése után alelnöke, Kamala Harris elvesztette a 2024-es elnökválasztást. A vereség után a demokrata szavazók körében ismét előtérbe kerültek az ideológiai kérdések, amelyek a pártvezetéssel szembeni kiábrándulással összekapcsolódva masszív elégedetlenségi hullámot indítottak el.
Ez a gyakorlatban azt jelentette, hogy a magasan képzett, a közélet iránt aktívan érdeklődő demokrata törzsszavazók egyre inkább olyan jelölteket kezdtek támogatni, akiket baloldalibbnak és harciasabbnak találtak a hatástalannak tartott pártelithez képest. Mindez párosult a fiatal szavazók körében különösen erős Izrael-ellenességgel, amely a progresszívek és a mérsékeltek közötti belháború egyik legélesebb frontvonalává vált. Különös iróniája a helyzetnek, hogy Biden 2024-es újraindulása mellett éppen az a Bernie Sanders és Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) tartott ki a legtovább, akik ma a leghangosabban bírálják a demokraták külpolitikai irányvonalát.
Az előválasztás időpontjának közeledtével egyre nyilvánvalóbb lett a balszél ereje. Előbb a közösségi médiában berobbanó Zohran Mamdani győzte le a veterán demokrata Andrew Cuomót a New York-i polgármesteri székért folytatott küzdelemben, amivel ő lett a város első muszlim vezetője. items.body_text:
Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools - Nearly One in Five in Prague
Prague Morning
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.
According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.
Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.
Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.
The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.
The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.
Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.
The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.
Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School
Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.
Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.
This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

items.body_text:
Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
Prague Morning
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.
McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.
The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.
Burgermeister prepares Czech debut
One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.
The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.
Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding
Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.
The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.
Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.
Five Guys adds another international brand
The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.
The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.
Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.
Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.
The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.
Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities
The expansion is not limited to international companies.
Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.
The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.
