items.title: Fire-hit Klongthom Center can’t be saved, says Chadchart
items.summary: Fire broke out again on Saturday afternoon at Klongthom Center in Bangkok, after a major blaze overnight caused extensive damage to the popular market for second-hand goods, electronics, spare parts and tools.
items.body_text:
Fire broke out again on Saturday afternoon at Klongthom Center in Bangkok, after a major blaze overnight caused extensive damage to the popular market for second-hand goods, electronics, spare parts and tools.
Black, grey and reddish-brown smoke began billowing from the top of the three-storey building at 2.30pm as firefighters deployed water trucks to contain hotspots and prevent flames from spreading.
Authorities are investigating materials that might have burned, and warning the public that the smoke may contain toxic gases or chemicals.
Black, grey and reddish-brown smoke billows from fire-hit Klongthom Center during efforts to contain remaining hotspots on Saturday. (Photo: Fire & Rescue Thailand)
After inspecting the scene on Worachak Road in Pom Prap Sattru Phai district, Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the building could not be salvaged.
“The damage is currently 100%, covering the entire four-rai site. Klongthom Center is probably no more,” he said. “The structure will have to be demolished because it has been severely damaged.”
He said Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) drone teams had surveyed the area, and images showed that the main building had completely collapsed from the inside.
Firefighters were using excavators to clear access routes and reach the interior to extinguish the remaining fires. The operation was being carried out with caution as the building’s structure had suffered extensive damage.
The market building contained various goods, including batteries, solar panels and some chemicals that could produce toxic substances when burned.
Smoke and dust from the fire also present a health hazard, with fine-dust particles, or PM2.5, measured at 630 microgrammes per cubic metre — considered extremely hazardous and far above Thailand’s national standard of 37.5 μg/m³.
People living or working near the site have been urged to wear protective N95 masks, while vulnerable groups should take extra precautions. The wind was expected to blow towards the northeast, the governor said.
Bangkok governor Chadchart Sittipunt monitors the situation at the site on Worachak Road in Pom Prap Sattru Phai in Bangkok on Saturday.
An initial inspection found that a sprinkler system in the building had not operated during the fire. Further checks were required.
The fire started at 8.42pm on Friday. The building began to collapse at 10.16pm and the blaze was finally brought under control at 5.32am on Saturday, according to the BMA’s Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation.
The fire was believed to have started on the first floor, where large quantities of electronic equipment, audio systems, IT products, LED equipment, solar panels and automotive accessories were stored. The materials provided substantial fuel, causing the blaze to burn for an extended period.
Klongthom Center had about 300 shop stalls and an estimated 100 operators, as some traders operated more than one stall. About 70 operators have so far registered to report losses, while the BMA was collecting information and assessing the extent of the damage. The total value of losses has yet to be determined.
For affected people seeking assistance, the Pom Prap Sattru Phai district office set up a registration point at the Phra Phiren Temple pavilion.
From Sunday onwards, applications can be submitted to the administration section on the second floor of the district office, also from 8am to 4pm.
Nearby commercial buildings affected by the fire included an 88-room dormitory and a warehouse storing plastic goods and phone equipment.
Nine people were injured and taken to various hospitals: four suffered smoke inhalation, three sustained cuts from broken glass, one suffered a shoulder injury after being struck by a falling concrete slab, and one fell from a height and suffered pain in both legs.
Police have been asked to help secure the area because the site contained large quantities of goods that could be vulnerable to theft. The area has been design

items.title: Forum warned about ‘takeover’ of country
items.summary: People’s Party leader Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut has warned that alleged irregularities in the 2024 Senate election were the starting point of an attempt to gain control of the country.
items.body_text:
People’s Party leader Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut has warned that alleged irregularities in the 2024 Senate election were the starting point of an attempt to gain control of the country.
Mr Natthaphong, the leader of the opposition in the House, made the remarks on Saturday while opening an opposition leaders’ forum at Parliament.
The forum was held after the Election Commission (EC) announced it would vote on the Senate election-rigging case on Sept 14.
Three former opposition leaders — Chaithawat Tulathon, Abhisit Vejjajiva and Cholnan Srikaew — also joined the forum, held under the theme “Thai Politics in a Crisis of Confidence: The Truth Society Demands Answers”.
Participants discussed scrutiny of the Senate selection process and the performance of independent organisations, for which senators play a major role in choosing members.
Mr Natthaphong said the forum was being held about 100 days after he first raised concerns about what he called the “blue regime” — blue being the colour of the coalition-leading Bhumjaithai Party.
He said he agreed with the description of the regime as having authoritarian characteristics, which contrasted with a democratic system that should have checks and balances and be accountable to the people.
“What we are seeing today is that independent organisations originate from senators who may have been organised or brought in through vote-rigging, and who have links to the political party currently leading the government,” he said. “That was why I pointed out at the time that the blue regime was taking over the country.”
He said Saturday’s forum was intended as a platform for former opposition leaders from different eras to voice their shared vision of a democratic political system, rather than an authoritarian system in which a particular group seeks to take control of the country.
“By holding forums like this … we are making what seems impossible increasingly difficult for them to deny,” People’s Party leader Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut tells participants at an opposition leaders’ forum at Parliament on Saturday. (Photo: People’s Party)
According to Mr Natthaphong, discussions at previous opposition forums had led many participants to a common conclusion that manipulation of the Senate election process represented the starting point of broader efforts to consolidate power.
He said the forum provided a platform for former opposition leaders from different eras to voice their shared vision of a democratic political system, rather than an authoritarian system in which a particular group seeks to take control of the country.
Addressing the ongoing investigation into the Senate selection process, the People’s Party leader acknowledged that many people viewed efforts to hold accountable those deemed involved as difficult, if not impossible.
Legal experts have said that a lot of the evidence provided to the Election Commission appeared circumstantial, and EC secretary-general Sawaeng Boonmee recently outlined three legal conditions that must be met for the body to send the case to court.
Mr Natthaphong said four of the EC’s seven members were selected by the current Senate, many of whose members are named in the investigation files. Questions have arisen regarding potential conflicts of interest, he said.
He said many people entered politics with idealistic ambitions to turn what appeared impossible into something that could no longer be denied.
“By holding forums like this every day and on every occasion, we are making what seems impossible increasingly difficult for them to deny,” he said of the government and its allies.
The opposition leader said the evidence that needed to be made undeniable included witnesses willing to provide information about the Senate election-rigging process, documentary evidence such as reservation slips, as well as video and other evidence showing that the locations and events in question actually existed.
He said the EC’s current role was not to determine guilt or innocence

items.title: Lost in Translation
items.summary: Amid a week of heavy debate about borrowing 400 billion baht, questions about the legitimacy of the Senate and vows to restore tourism numbers to pre-Covid levels, an admittedly trivial exercise initiated by Thai officials ended up speaking volumes.
items.body_text:
Amid a week of heavy debate about borrowing 400 billion baht, questions about the legitimacy of the Senate and vows to restore tourism numbers to pre-Covid levels, an admittedly trivial exercise initiated by Thai officials ended up speaking volumes.
With plans to introduce a “tourism fee” of 450 baht on foreigners arriving to Thailand sometime in the near future, the government announced it would be taking views from both Thai nationals and foreigners via an online public hearing.
Until Sept 28 of this year, the 27-question survey is available to be filled out on the law website of the Council of State’s Digital Government Development Agency.
In a rather telling turn, however, the dense questionnaire is presented completely in Thai, in a rather unintuitive format even for this citizen of the nation.
This shouldn’t be an obstacle at a time when AI stands constantly at the ready to translate, summarise or even dramatise any information for easy consumption.
The webpage almost comedically underlines this fact by presenting a classic language toggle in its top right corner that users will quickly find is not clickable. Instead, when hovering over the toggle, visitors are presented with a message, again completely in Thai, that asks them to “Right click so that your browser may translate this page.”
Depending on your native language, the browser you use and the language settings you’ve enabled, it might take a few minutes of trial and error to get started. After that it’s plain sailing.
Still, how is it that a team of officials intent on hearing the views of Thailand’s millions of potential visitors on a matter with a direct impact on their travel plans commissioned, vetted and approved a survey in a language spoken by less than one percent of the global population?
The questionnaire allows respondents to answer as representatives of state agencies, private entities or just as general members of the public, likely the catch-all for individual foreigners who wish to weigh in on the move.
Hits and misses
In terms of carrying out a “public hearing”, the page is effective in its function. The first “agree/disagree” question posed asks directly, “Do you agree with a fee being collected from foreign tourists travelling in the nation to be used in support of the management and development of tourism, including the provision of insurance to foreign tourists while they are journeying through the country?”
Other questions appear to have further-reaching significance. The fourth question asks for input on how to define a “foreign tourist”, seeking agreement on whether or not such a status is “exclusive to non-Thais temporarily entering the country for travel purposes that do not generate employment or compensation.”
Would enough disagreement with this characterisation lead to a redefining of what a tourist is in Thailand? Could it become a precedent for dealing with issues involving foreigners in the future? Is a tourist not already a legally defined term that was not awaiting further discussion on an informal survey?
Several of the questions presented are concerned with defining different terms, including Land and Maritime Checkpoints, and Operator. Again, would responses here have any impact on the matters referenced?
The tenth question, allowing for multiple answers, does not even seem relevant, asking if the fee should apply to entrants such as holders of diplomatic passports and holders of work permits, groups that definitely do not qualify as tourists.
In fact, the average person would have trouble answering many of the questions, which appear intended only for bureaucrats or lawyers. Example: “Do you agree with the designation of the Chairman of the National Tourism Policy Committee as the acting authority under this announcement? (Clause 12, paragraph one)”

No injuries were reported and the cause of the fire is under investigation.
SINGAPORE: A fire that affected about 3ha of vegetation near Seletar Link was extinguished on Saturday (Aug 29), the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) said.
In response to CNA's query, SCDF said it was alerted to a fire near Seletar Link and Seletar South Link around 11.05am.
"The fire involved vegetation measuring about 150m by 200m," it said, adding that the flames were extinguished using two water jets and an unmanned firefighting machine. The affected area is roughly equivalent to 4 football fields.
A Punggol resident, Mr Shawn Cheong, said he reported the fire at around 11.20am after seeing smoke and flames in the area while driving by. When returning around 3.30pm, he saw multiple SCDF and police vehicles still at the scene.
“When I was driving back, I thought the firefighting would have been over,” Mr Cheong told CNA, adding that he was shocked as he initially thought the blaze was not big.
SCDF did not state what time the fire was extinguished.
There were no reported injuries, and the cause of the fire is under investigation, it said.

items.title: War weighs on Iran's economy as US intensifies sanctions
items.body_text:
War weighs on Iran's economy as US intensifies sanctions
DUBAI: Iranian leaders are acknowledging the economic toll of war with the United States, with the supreme leader urging the government to address the hardship and the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by a third due to the American sanctions and blockade.
Yet Tehran signalled no retreat on Saturday (Aug 29), vowing to withstand US pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it said was control over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets.
The government said in a statement on state media that addressing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war was a central focus, including curbing inflation, managing markets, creating jobs, directing investment towards domestic production and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.
Six months after the US and Israel launched the war, negotiations are at an impasse, and US President Donald Trump's administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an "economic D-Day".
SANCTIONS COMPOUND TOLL ON IRAN'S ECONOMY
Washington has warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, though the Treasury Department stopped short of imposing penalties against major Iranian trade partners such as China and India, which could have repercussions for the US and global economies.
The Treasury imposed sanctions on Egypt's Banque Misr for doing business with Tehran, proposing a rule that would cut off the bank's branches in the United Arab Emirates from dollar transactions.
Egypt's central bank said it and the foreign ministry were in contact with US officials concerning the matter, adding the measure was limited to Banque Misr UAE’s US dollar transactions with correspondent banks only.
Banque Misr said later in a statement it was reviewing the US Treasury notice, adding that its branch in the UAE continued to provide banking services to its customers in line with applicable rules and procedures.
The US also issued sanctions targeting an entity based in Hong Kong and a person linked to Iran's Bank Melli, according to a notice on the Treasury website.
The sanctions drive compounds the toll of the war on Iran's economy, where annual inflation hit 66 per cent last month.
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei - who has not been seen publicly since he was injured in the initial Feb 28 attack that killed his father and former Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei - called on the government to tackle the economic hardship.
"There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services," according to a written statement attributed to Khamenei.
President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35 per cent because of US sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the US and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.
IRAN VOWS TO PURSUE DIPLOMACY AND DEFENCE
With the US focused on its economic pressure campaign, others have sought to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed Abdulrahman Al Thani met with Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday. He said he had stressed during the meeting the importance of returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as "creative".
In Saturday's statement, Iran said diplomacy and defence were "two complementary, coordinated and inseparable wings" for protecting the country's national interests, security and territorial integrity. It said it would pursue both tracks in a balanced manner.

items.title: Bezzecchi shatters lap record to beat Marquez brothers to Aragon GP pole
items.body_text:
Bezzecchi shatters lap record to beat Marquez brothers to Aragon GP pole
Aug 29 : Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi became the first rider to crack the one minute and 45 seconds barrier at MotorLand, snatching pole position for the Aragon Grand Prix and ending Marc Marquez's bid for a hat-trick of poles at the circuit on Saturday.
The Italian initially set the pace with a time of 1:44.984 before going even faster with another lap record of 1:44.962, leaving Ducati's Marquez unable to match the Aprilia rider's scorching pace.
Marquez, who has won seven MotoGP races at Aragon, will start alongside Bezzecchi on the front row despite a heart-stopping moment while braking on a flying lap. His brother Alex Marquez, of Gresini Racing, completes the front row.
"Well, it was a positive morning overall... Obviously, the qualifying was good fun. I'm happy to be fast and to grab the pole position," Bezzecchi said.
"Now the real job starts... We start in a good place, but Marc and Alex are both super fast in terms of pace with both tyres, so it's going to be a tough fight. But we are enjoying and let's see what we can do."
Reigning world champion Marc Marquez accepted that Bezzecchi had the faster bike.
"Marco, at the moment, has a better pace than us, so sometimes you cannot do anything. You just try to do your best and it's what we are doing," he said.
"I pushed hard on that brake point, maybe too much and I had that moment. I feel that I can keep a constant pace, but Marco basically has a bit faster pace."
Trackhouse Racing's Raul Fernandez was fourth-fastest and he will line up on the second row with Aprilia's Jorge Martin and KTM's Pedro Acosta.
The third row features VR46 Racing's Fabio Di Giannantonio, Ducati's Francesco Bagnaia and LCR Honda's Johann Zarco, who made a memorable return from a knee injury sustained in a crash at the Catalan Grand Prix in May.

items.body_text:
Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
Harare - A minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe, killing at least 27 people, police said Aug 29, in the latest deadly road crash to hit the country.
The crash occurred at around 1830 GMT on Aug 28 (2.30am, Aug 29, Singapore time) near Chivhu, about 140km south of the capital Harare, police said.
The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus, which was carrying worshippers to a conference.
Both vehicles were carrying an “unknown” number of passengers, police said. Seven people were injured in the crash.
Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell, with the truck coming to rest on the opposite side of the road.
The crash occurred in a flat, remote stretch of road, with low vegetation lining the roadside and open terrain beyond.
Traffic accidents are common in Zimbabwe, where roads are riddled with potholes due to years of underfunding and neglect, and driving standards can be poor.
For everyday transport, many Zimbabweans rely on the privately run minibus taxis, known locally as kombi, but they are often criticised for overloading.
In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in the south, while earlier that month a woman and her five children died when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa. AFP

- Armed Druze factions in Sweida province blocked students from travelling to government-run exam centres, demanding tests be held in Druze-controlled areas due to security concerns.
- The Damascus-appointed governor condemned the move, calling it political manipulation that harms students' futures, while about 150 students managed to sit exams by avoiding obstacles.

Sweida, Syria - Armed factions in Syria’s Druze-majority Sweida province have blocked students from travelling to sit official exams, demanding they be held instead in the areas they control, drawing condemnation from the Damascus-appointed governor on Aug 29.
Sweida city and other parts of the southern province are run by local armed groups and are the last areas outside the grasp of Syria’s new Islamist authorities, who have been trying to establish control over the entire country after toppling long-time ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Tensions have run high ever since clashes in 2025 between the Druze and government-aligned forces that spiralled into some of the worst internecine violence the country had witnessed since Assad’s fall.
The authorities had scheduled an exam session for Aug 29 in the government-controlled north of the province for students who were unable to take the test two months ago due to the ongoing tensions.
But Druze fighters in Shahba, north of Sweida city, said in a statement on Aug 28 that “all roads are completely closed to the movement of students and proctors to examination centres outside the area”, insisting that tests should be held in their areas instead, citing security concerns.
Sweida governor Mustafa al-Bakkur condemned the move on Aug 29, saying: “Outlaw gangs are working to make the future of Sweida’s students a political bargaining chip to be manipulated as they please.”
He said that around 150 students were still able to sit their exams, some of them having left Druze-controlled areas days prior to avoid any obstacles.
One 18-year-old student told AFP she was on a bus in Sweida city hoping for the road to open when “an armed group arrived and threatened the students”.
“Some members of these factions fired shots into the air to intimidate and frighten the students” after they insisted on heading north, she added, requesting anonymity out of fear for her safety.
The education ministry said in a statement that it “regrets that not all of our students were able to reach the examination centres”.
In July 2025, clashes erupted in Sweida between Druze factions and Bedouin fighters, with security forces intervening on the side of the Bedouins along with other tribal groups.
In the end, more than 2,000 people were killed, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor. A committee formed by the Syrian government said it had documented the killing of 1,760 people.
Government forces and their allies were accused at the time of executing civilians and other abuses, and Damascus in July said it began trying suspects over the violence.
Israel, which also has a Druze population, intervened militarily during the clashes with strikes in Sweida and Damascus, saying it was defending the minority community.
One Druze leader, Hikmat al-Hijri, went so far as to say on Aug 24 that his community is “an integral part of the State of Israel”. AFP

items.body_text:
US military families ride 'roller coaster of emotions' over six months of Iran war
Aug 29 - Since the United States went to war with Iran six months ago, Courtney Sanders has been helping soldiers’ families fill the gaps left by their loved ones.
There are school pickups to coordinate, lost incomes to supplement — and the ever-present separation anxiety.
“It's like being on pins and needles all of the time,” Sanders said.
She leads the Chicagoland chapter of Blue Star Families, the nation's largest nonprofit serving military families, and her own daughters are in the U.S. Navy. They have served in various overseas locations over the past six months, including the Middle East.
The U.S. has more than 50,000 troops stationed across the region and has deployed thousands of additional Marines and sailors to support the war effort. Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed in the conflict and more than 750 wounded.
During the war's on-and-off fighting, shuttle diplomacy and failed peace talks, military families have experienced a “roller coaster of emotions,” Sanders said. “The moment that you feel you're able to take a breath, you get gut-punched again.”
These are familiar pressures for the partners and children, mothers and fathers, of American troops. But the suddenness of the Iranian conflict, and its fitful pace, have had a compounding effect, relatives told Reuters.
In a Blue Star Families poll of some 200 active-duty military families in early March, 81% reported elevated stress from the Iran conflict.
The group has responded by stepping up its programming, creating online resource hubs, hosting webinars and in-person meet-ups, and matching military spouses going through a deployment for the first time with those who have been through it before.
Many service members' deployments have been extended unexpectedly.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier went more than 200 days without a port call — a modern-day record, according to Democratic lawmakers — and military outlets reported suicide attempts and declining morale among its 5,000 sailors and Marines. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the reports “completely misrepresented” the conditions on board.
Some military families find themselves in financial straits.
National Guard members, for example, often work regular jobs when they are not deployed. The sudden loss of their main paycheck can make it hard for those left behind to keep food on the table, Sanders said.
"There is a huge misconception in the civilian world that if you are in the military, all of your bills are taken care of,” she said. “And that is just frankly not true.”
In a statement, the Pentagon said: "We see these families (and) we hear their concerns. We will do whatever is necessary to provide the resources, assistance, and stability they need and deserve during these challenging times."
'A LOT OF EMOTIONS'
Shannon, an Army spouse and mother of three in North Carolina who requested Reuters use only her first name for security reasons, tries to tune out the news and the political debate surrounding the war.
In February, her husband deployed to the region with five days' notice and could only contact her sporadically for the first several months.
Although they have maintained near-daily communication since June, "there are a lot of emotions,” Shannon said, “especially when people are dying over there.”
Her children started therapy over the summer. She tries to be strong in front of them, but cries sometimes when they’re not around.
Soon after her husband's deployment, Shannon joined an Army-sponsored soldier-and-family "readiness group" within her husband's unit, helping organize meal trains and other support for family members in need.
"Every day is not going to be a great day, but you've gotta just keep going and keep yourself busy," she said.

items.title: Population to plummet, council warns
items.body_text:
- 
            Population to plummet, council warnsINCREASING IMBALANCE: The percentage of working-age people is expected to shrink to 42.3% of the population, while older people would comprise 52.9%, the agency said
  - By Crystal Hsu / Staff reporter
 Taiwan’s population is projected to shrink by almost half over the next five decades, intensifying labor shortages and placing a growing drag on economic growth as the technology-intensive economy confronts a rapidly aging workforce. The population is expected to fall to 12.15 million by 2075, a 48 percent decline from this year, National Development Council projections released yesterday showed. The decline would fundamentally alter Taiwan’s workforce. From 2037, more than half of the working-age population is projected to be aged between 45 and 64, signaling the end of an era when the economy could rely on a relatively large labor force. Children climb on playground equipment at a park in Taipei yesterday.Photo: CNA The shift threatens to challenge Taiwan’s growth model, which depends on a broad manufacturing workforce and a growing supply of highly skilled workers to support its semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries. A shrinking pool of workers could make recruitment increasingly difficult, while a growing elderly population would add pressure on social spending and public finances. The projections also point to a deeper demographic problem — Taiwan is not only losing its population, but failing to replenish it, the council said. It lowered its long-term fertility assumptions after the fertility rate fell to a record low 0.695 last year, significantly below previous estimates. The number of women aged 20 to 49 has declined since peaking in 2005, while the proportion of married women in that age group has also fallen. The shrinking pool of potential mothers is making a sustained recovery in births increasingly difficult, it said. Taiwan’s population is projected to fall below 20 million in 2045, dropping to 19.98 million. People aged 65 or older are expected to account for 37 percent of the population, while the working-age population would shrink to 57.9 percent and children to just 5.2 percent, the council said. By 2075, the imbalance would be even more pronounced, with older people projected to comprise 52.9 percent of the population, working-age people 42.3 percent and children 4.8 percent, it said. The dependency ratio — the number of children and elderly people relative to those of working age — is projected to rise from 55.2 dependents for every 100 working-age people to 136.6 by 2075, the council said. The potential support ratio is expected to fall below one, suggesting less than one working-age person for every person aged 65 or older, it said. The government is preparing the economy for a permanently smaller workforce. It has established a population strategy task force, and in May launched 18 measures covering childbirth support, childcare, education, workplace policies and housing. Additional policy packages would target elderly people, talent development across all age groups and the recruitment of overseas talent, the council said. For businesses, the implications extend beyond hiring. Companies are likely to face greater pressure to raise labor force participation among elderly people, attract workers from overseas, and accelerate automation and productivity gains.

items.title: CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other two
items.body_text:
- 
            CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other twoCONDEMNED: The KMT slammed the rejections, saying the CEC decided on behalf of 23 million people, while the TPP said it brought shame to Taiwan’s democratic system
  - By Hsu Yung-ching / Staff reporter
 The Central Election Commission (CEC) yesterday announced it has approved holding a referendum on nuclear power, but rejected proposals on caning and traffic fines. The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 14 approved three referendums: introducing caning as a criminal punishment, abolishing the government’s nuclear-free homeland policy and using traffic fines to improve road safety. The commission met for more than two and a half hours, and ruled that the referendum on caning did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法), CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said. Central Election Commission Chairman Michael You speaks at a news conference in Taipei yesterday.Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times The caning proposal, put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeks to introduce caning as a punishment for sexual assault, crimes against children, large-scale fraud and aggravated fraud. However, caning or similar forms of corporal punishment are not recognized under Taiwan’s criminal justice system, You said. The CEC therefore determined that the proposal amounted to creating new legislative principles, and was not a referendum on the initiation or repeal of a major policy, as defined by the act, he added. The proposal involves using state power to inflict physical pain on prisoners and is considered by many countries to be cruel, inhuman and a violation of human dignity, he said. That would contravene the Act Governing Execution of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (公民與政治權利國際公約及經濟社會文化權利國際公約施行法), which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, he added. Of the eight CEC members, seven voted that the caning proposal did not qualify as a referendum, said You, who chaired the meeting, adding that he did not cast a vote. Regarding the Taiwan People’s Party’s (TPP) proposed referendum on earmarking traffic fines exclusively for road-related purposes, four commission members found that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said. The commission held three rounds of voting, with the same 4-3 split each time, he added. As for the proposal to repeal Taiwan’s nuclear-free homeland policy, six CEC members supported the referendum, with one abstention, You said. The CEC ruled that the proposal meets the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said, adding that the referendum vote would be held on Nov. 28, alongside the local elections. The KMT caucus condemned the CEC’s decision to reject the two proposals, saying that referendums exist to give people a direct say when a country faces major disputes over public policy. “Yet what has happened now is that whether people want to vote no longer matters, and neither does whether the Legislative Yuan approves the proposal,” it said. “Instead the CEC has decided on behalf of 23 million people: ‘You are not entitled to answer this question.’” “Is this direct democracy, or the direct confiscation of democracy?” it asked. The TPP slammed You, saying he had claimed that “referendums submitted by the Legislative Yuan should be approved in principle and rejected only as an exception.” “Yet he has now turned that exception into a pretext for arbitrarily expanding his powers, abandoning his principles as an academic, enabling the ruling party to flout the law and obstructing the public’s right to initiate referendums,” it said. “Such actions have brought shame on Taiwan’s democratic constitutional system.” Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han

items.title: Prosecutors indict nine in Dr Shine hidden camera case
items.body_text:
- 
            Prosecutors indict nine in Dr Shine hidden camera case
  - By Wang Ting-chuan and Jake Chung / Staff reporter, with staff writer
 Prosecutors yesterday indicted nine people for allegedly installing hidden surveillance cameras in eight Dr Shine (光澤) clinics in Taipei and New Taipei City, and secretly recording more than 300 patients — including four minors — while they were exposed. Investigations into other branches allegedly involved in the case are still ongoing. The New Taipei City District Prosecutors’ Office is seeking a prison term of 16 years for Dr Shine group operations manager Chen Chih-min (陳志敏), 14 years for company information department head Tang Yung-chieh (唐詠傑) and seven years for surveillance camera supplier Chang Chao-ming (張朝銘). A branch of the Dr Shine cosmetics chain is pictured in New Taipei City in an undated photograph.Photo: Hsu Sheng-lun, Taipei Times They also proposed seven years for Dr Shine employee Chiang Chin-wei (江勁緯) and unspecified prison terms for five other employees embroiled in the case. Chen and Tang had abused clients’ trust, shown no remorse, offered no public apology and attempted to deceive police into believing that the devices had been removed years earlier, so they should receive severe sentences, the prosecutors’ office said in the indictment. Prosecutors also called on Dr Shine owner Wang Chao-huei (王朝輝) to return to Taiwan to face investigation over the scandal. Wang traveled to China before the incident came to light, but has allegedly shown no sign of willingly returning to Taiwan, even after a wanted notice was issued for him. Chen and Tang allegedly installed surveillance cameras disguised as smoke detectors or sensor-activated lighting at two Dr Shine clinics in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋); and one each in Sanxia District (三峽), Sanchong District (三重) and Sinjhuang District (新莊), prosecutors said. They installed the same devices at clinics in Taipei’s Guting District (古亭), Daan District (大安) and Songshan District (松山), they added. Tang allegedly created a Line group that included Chen and others, and used it to direct efforts to remove surveillance cameras from all branches between May 5 and May 8, prosecutors said. The installation of cameras allegedly gave Chen and Tang access to private moments when patients were exposed, severely infringing on people’s constitutionally guaranteed rights to privacy and self-determination, prosecutors added.

items.body_text:
Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages.
The number of missing soared close to 3,000 Saturday, latest figures from both countries showed, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Those that made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonising wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous”, and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
Compounding the search for the missing have been fears of further flooding in affected areas.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location”, saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side”.
In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding, before saying the threat had eased.
State news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area.
‘All swept away’
On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than a hundred trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP.
Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists — seven people died and 554 remain missing, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Pilgrimage route
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.

items.body_text:
China removes high-ranking officers Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli from key military body
In January though, the defence ministry said that Zhang and Liu were “suspected of serious violations of discipline and the law”, a common euphemism for corruption.
China removed two high-ranking officers from the country’s main military body on Friday, state media reported, seven months after it was announced that Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were being investigated for “serious violations of the law”.
Zhang’s position as the more senior of two vice chairmen on the Central Military Commission (CMC) had made him China’s highest-ranked general.
In January though, the defence ministry said that Zhang and Liu were “suspected of serious violations of discipline and the law”, a common euphemism for corruption.
The announcement fit into the sweeping anti-graft drive that has defined President Xi Jinping’s time in power — but Zhang’s fall from grace in particular shocked observers, given his seniority and the perception he was close to Xi.
On Friday, state news agency Xinhua said in a report on a meeting of the standing committee of China’s parliament that “the meeting decided to remove Zhang Youxia from the post of Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission of the People’s Republic of China”.
Liu, who was chief of staff of the CMC’s joint staff department, which oversees combat planning, was also removed, it said.
The CMC is China’s most important military decision-making body, chaired by Xi.
Technically, there are two — a state CMC and a Communist Party CMC.
“For practical purposes, however, they are treated as one (and) the same in (China’s) bureaucracy,” Asia Society’s Lyle Morris has written.
Friday’s announcement relates to Zhang and Liu’s positions in the state CMC rather than the Party one.
Their removal will leave the CMC, which is supposed to have seven members, with only two known representatives: Xi and anti-corruption chief Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang and Liu’s whereabouts are unknown, and no details have been given regarding the accusations against them.
At the time the investigation was announced, an editorial in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Daily said the two men had “seriously trampled on and undermined the system of ultimate responsibility resting with the CMC chairman” — that is, Xi.

items.body_text:
A Hong Kong court has found a police officer not guilty of indecent assault after rejecting the testimony of his accuser.
Officer Ng Ka‑wai pleaded not guilty when he appeared at the Kowloon City Magistrates’ Courts on Friday.
According to the case details, the 41-year-old allegedly touched the thigh of a female informant and opened a nude photo of her without her consent inside Tsim Sha Tsui Police Station on December 20 last year.
The informant was in the station to report being blackmailed with nude photos and defrauded of HK$1.6 million. Police then arranged for Ng to assist the informant in giving a statement.
According to the prosecution, the informant told Ng that a fraudster had sent her nude photos of herself using the “View Once” feature on WhatsApp to blackmail her. She then handed her phone to Ng, who she alleged opened one of the photos without her permission.
She also alleged that Ng asked her to stand with him to check online bank statements, and then touched her thigh three times.
However, Magistrate Arthur Lam said on Friday that what the woman told the court was not consistent with her written statements.
For example, the woman told the court that she only realised a suspected “View Once” nude photo had been opened after getting her phone back from the defendant. But during cross-examination, the defence cited her written statement, in which she said that the defendant showed her the nude photos on her mobile and commented on them while viewing them.
Lam called the informant’s explanations unconvincing, and the court therefore did not accept her testimony. He ruled that Ng was not guilty of the charge and awarded him legal costs.
A conviction for indecent assault in Hong Kong carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment.

Second face-to-face talks this year to come as leaders of China and Russia visit Kyrgyzstan for Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit

items.body_text:
Japan probes 39kg of bread dumped in national park
The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found
A total of 39kg (85 lbs) of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why.
The loaves were left near crash barriers in Daisen-Oki National Park in Tottori Prefecture between August 14 and 20. The incident has prompted the spread of fake images and videos attempting to link the dumping to a sharp increase in bear encounters in Japan over the past year.
“When I first heard of the reports, my head was full of question marks,” said Koji Iwaihara, director of the Natural Parks Foundation’s Tottori branch.
The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found. The foundation later came to believe the bread had been left to feed animals after 1.3kg of chicken was found in the same area.
Bread was also found scattered around the prefecture’s Hakuto coast, but the brand appears to be different from that found in the national park. Neither the bread nor the chicken was poisoned.

items.title: Scientists probe if herpes virus is killing sardines off South Africa
items.summary: Scientists in South Africa are investigating why masses of sardines have washed up dead or dying along parts of the country’s west and south coast – and if a herpes virus detected in the fish is responsible. The mass mortality of sardines this month has so far stumped the country’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, though scientists have come to at least one conclusion: it is the first time that the virus in question – pilchard herpesvirus, or PHV – has been identified in...
items.body_text:
Scientists probe if herpes virus is killing sardines off South Africa
Pilchard herpesvirus is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health
Scientists in South Africa are investigating why masses of sardines have washed up dead or dying along parts of the country’s west and south coast – and if a herpes virus detected in the fish is responsible.
The mass mortality of sardines this month has so far stumped the country’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, though scientists have come to at least one conclusion: it is the first time that the virus in question – pilchard herpesvirus, or PHV – has been identified in sardines off South Africa.
PHV, which was linked to two mass sardine mortality events in Australia in the 1990s, can cause inflammation and thickening of sardines’ gills, which interferes with their oxygen uptake, according to the South African environment department.
Sardines and pilchards are the same type of fish, with sardines being the younger, smaller ones.
PHV is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health, the department said, and its detection does not mean that healthy sardines caught commercially or canned sardine products are unsafe to eat.
Dozens of sardines taken from affected areas, some dead and some alive, are being examined by scientists at the South African Institute for Aquatic Biodiversity and a local university.

items.body_text:
新竹棒球場案林智堅不起訴 曾翰揚：政治操作謊言不敵司法檢驗
新竹棒球場。（資料照，記者洪美秀攝）
新竹市立棒球場案前市長林智堅獲不起訴，市議員參選人曾翰揚稱，市長高虹安為撈取政治利益，不惜將竹市過去幾年的重大公共建設全面抹黑。用鋪天蓋地的政治文宣、敲鑼打鼓的記者會，把守護兒童健康的市立兒童醫院和新竹棒球場形容得十惡不赦。但政治操作的謊言，終究敵不過司法與法院的檢驗。
他說，先前民眾黨議員指控，新竹市立兒童醫院容積率暴增、涉嫌圖利。結果新竹地檢署已查明，該案不僅查無不法，整體規劃更是完全合法合規、造福大新竹地區兒童醫療的實質建設。
民眾黨議員用政治口水抹黑醫療專業，更直接被最高行政法院狠狠打臉。被藍白陣營當作政治提款機、政治秀場的新竹棒球場統包案，經新竹地檢署長達4年的嚴格偵辦，調閱所有金流、帳目與工程通訊。結果林智堅及相關公務員全數不起訴。
他認為，這證明過去幾年政客口中的大秘寶，是徹頭徹尾的政治獵巫。而回顧桃園地方法院判決，法院認證高虹安市府在過去處理球場時，未依法辦理驗收就盲目開挖，甚至「阻礙驗收、破壞現場、拒絕配合法院依法發動的司法鑑定」。那場大張旗鼓、耗費公帑請來美國草皮專家挖球場，不過是齣昂貴的公關秀。
因高虹安市府的行政失能與惡意拖延，本該在改善後就能正常啟用的棒球場，被無限期封鎖、反覆開挖，導致後續改善工程面臨無止境的重修與追加預算，且城市的形象，也被政治惡鬥摧毀殆盡。

items.body_text:
（獨家）陳盈潔離世當晚首還原！許常德交棒于美人 死訊公布內幕曝光
于美人接手成為陳盈潔對外發言窗口，許常德今揭背後原因。（記者陳奕全攝）
〔記者傅茗渝／台北報導〕台語歌壇「大姐大」陳盈潔本月12日晚間7點病逝，享壽72歲，告別式將於明（30）日舉行。當時死訊曝光後，是由主持人于美人第一時間對外證實，也讓不少人好奇，過去長期替陳盈潔處理醫療、善款等事宜的許常德，怎麼噤聲了？于美人、許常德今（29）日接受本報訪問，首度還原兩人早在3個月前就已完成「交棒」，許常德更透露陳盈潔離世當晚，他其實就在醫院，親眼見證陳盈潔人生最後一程。
于美人透露，今年5月31日替陳盈潔舉辦「搭上火箭前跟大家說再見音樂會」時，許常德就在台上宣布，「他的工作就到這邊，以後所有跟陳盈潔有關的，就由我當窗口。」她表示，當時雙方就已把工作分配好，希望未來有任何真實、確定的消息，都統一由她對外公布。
許常德（左）透露自己較情緒化，因此將陳盈潔後續對外事宜交由於美人處理。（記者陳奕全攝）
許常德也坦言，主動交棒其實與自己的個性有關，「我覺得我比較情緒化，因為我沒有辦法面對這個問題。」相較之下，于美人更有處理相關事務的經驗，且粉專有多達118萬人追蹤，因此才決定將對外發言工作交給她。
談起陳盈潔離世當晚，許常德當時人在電影院看電影，途中正巧收到醫師通知，「他說差不多、差不多了」，雖然醫師當下僅表示可能就是這一、兩天，但他一聽立刻離開電影院趕往醫院。
未料許常德抵達病房時，才一走進門，就看到醫師、護理師從簾子後方走出來，醫護人員也已準備替陳盈潔整理身體。他回憶當時陳盈潔的弟弟就在一旁低著頭輕語，他看見眼前一幕，立刻明白發生了什麼事，便退到病房外，獨自靜下來撰寫要給外界的文字。
許常德表示，文字寫完沒多久，陳盈潔弟弟走出來告知，姊姊已在晚間7點離開，而他清楚記得，當時時間約是7點05分，隨即便將寫好的內容傳給于美人，由她正式向外界公布死訊。
陪著陳盈潔走完最後一程，他感嘆，自己似乎總在一些重要友人的人生最後階段，剛好有機會陪在身邊，「好像冥冥中，我有一個緣分，可以跟她們在最後一個階段在旁邊。」他也透露，陳盈潔後期身體狀況已十分虛弱，他多次到醫院探望，陳盈潔甚至無法拿電話、無法說話，「我跟她沒有講過半句話，一個字都沒有。」每次見面，她只能睜大眼睛看著他，直到離世前約兩個月，才終於有了一次令他難忘的明確反應。
當時陳盈潔一連握了許常德3次手，讓他當下驚覺好友仍能回應自己，也正是那次互動，讓他下定決心替陳盈潔再辦最後一場音樂會。未料5月31日活動落幕兩天後，陳盈潔又因病情插管，最後再撐過兩個多月，於本月12日告別人世。

items.body_text:
（直擊）中島健人想吃台灣粉絲！許願前進小巨蛋：你們會跟我一起嗎？
中島健人閃亮亮登場，這種桃紅色鏡然也這麼適合他。（大鴻藝術提供）
〔記者廖俐惠／台北報導〕日本男星中島健人出道15年首次亞巡迴《"IDOL1ST 中島健人" LIVE TOUR 2026》今明（29、30日）兩天將在新莊Zepp New Taipei舉行，兩天吸引4400名粉絲朝聖，其中子瑜媽媽也被目擊坐在貴賓席支持，從頭看到尾，手上還拿著應援手燈「IDOLICの魔法」，非常投入在中島健人的演出中。
中島健人今天以埃及風的金黃色服裝登場，臉上還戴著面具，神秘感十足，他一連獻唱《SOL1ST》、《IDOLIC》以及《MONTAGE》開場，甩掉面具、露出帥臉，掀起全場尖叫聲。他用華語大喊：「好久不見！我回來了！你們有想我嗎？我也很想你們！」中島健人表示，很開心能夠回到台北，「這是我第一次的亞洲巡迴演出就在台北，我真的非常想念大家，這次的主題是《IDOL1ST》，我3000年前就是偶像，所以搞不好我們3000年前就與大家相遇，所以我要說好久不見。」
中島健人是什麼法老王，竟然能把Zepp變成兩層樓，真的是amazing。（大鴻藝術提供）
接著他演出《Celeste》、《Can't Stop》、《Fiction Love》時，換穿喜氣洋洋的金蔥桃紅色，整個人全身上下都閃閃發光，還拿出紅遍迷妹的應援手燈「IDOLICの魔法」在舞台上玩遊戲，為演出增添趣味。中島健人表演到夯曲之一的《最初はキュン！》（Saishowa Kyun!），大玩「猜拳」以及「心動」的諧音哏。
中場talking環節，中島健人表示：「去年的演唱會非常有趣，今年能夠再次來真的好高興，我在這裡獲得很多能量。我很開心見到你們，昨天很多人來接機，我想說『難道我是大明星嗎？』我非常高興，我為了這次專場準備很多。」
撩粉無極限的他，一字一句都在撩粉絲，「喜歡我的應援魔法棒的舉手？喜歡手槍型應援棒的舉手？喜歡Kenty的舉手？」、「我喜歡你們，比小籠包還喜歡」、「（粉絲）推薦滷肉飯、推薦麵，那在吃之前，我可以先吃掉你們嗎？」每一句話都撩動人心。
中島健人提到，在演出前接受台灣媒體訪問，繼上一次記者送他青眼白龍卡之後，今天又收到一張，「他們說明年來會再送我一張，集齊3張青眼白龍就會變成青眼究極龍！」粉絲都很希望他總有一天能站上小巨蛋，「那是我的夢想，你們會跟我一起去嗎？」現場粉絲大聲歡呼。
「死亡芭比粉」也就只有中島健人能駕馭，現場宛如電影《芭比》。（大鴻藝術提供）
上一次他演唱周杰倫的歌曲，這一次則獻唱王心凌的《當你》，中島健人分享：「其實我準備了一個禮物，我現在很緊張，這是我第一次唱這首歌，是一個台灣歌曲。」前奏一下就掀起歡呼聲，中島健人唱得更是相當標準，讓粉絲又驚又喜。中島健人也坦言：「我真的很努力練習了，希望有傳達給大家，其實我緊張到快吐了！」
中島健人開場化身「埃及王子」，甩掉面具露出帥臉，全場粉絲爆出尖叫聲。（大鴻藝術提供）
接著他帶來《鬼事》以及與木谷龍也合唱的《Fatal》，再度炒熱現場氣氛，最後穿著黑色吊嘎以《Frequency》為演出暫時畫下句點。安可期間，粉絲整齊演唱《picaresque》，中島健人再度登台，也跟著演唱《picaresque》，現場十分溫馨，再來穿水藍色服裝演唱《JUST KENTY☆》、《CANDY》，最後以《Uni:verse》為演唱會畫下圓滿句點，螢幕上亮出他手寫的中文字：「謝謝台北的U:nity，希望今後也能和你一起創造歡樂的Kenty世界，愛台北U:nity。」

items.title: As won crashes, rural North Koreans rush to buy dollars
items.summary: A growing number of people in rural North Korea are converting their spare cash into U.S. dollars or Chinese yuan, as fears grow that the North Korean won is rapidly losing value, Daily NK has learned. Even in farming communities that once showed little interest in foreign currency, the belief that holding onto North Korean […]
items.body_text:
A growing number of people in rural North Korea are converting their spare cash into U.S. dollars or Chinese yuan, as fears grow that the North Korean won is rapidly losing value, Daily NK has learned. Even in farming communities that once showed little interest in foreign currency, the belief that holding onto North Korean won “means taking a loss” is spreading.
According to a Daily NK source in North Pyongan province on Wednesday, people in rural areas such as Ryongchon and Tongchang counties have increasingly been traveling to nearby cities to exchange even small amounts of North Korean won for dollars or yuan. Even when the sum is small, people believe holding foreign currency, rather than the domestic won, better protects the value of their savings.
In the past, farming communities had little occasion to use foreign currency in everyday transactions, making them relatively insensitive to exchange rate swings compared with city dwellers. This was especially true in mountainous areas, where jangmadang, the informal markets that have become the backbone of North Korea’s economy since the 1990s, open only about once every ten days, and trade largely takes the form of barter or won transactions, leaving little chance to encounter foreign currency at all.
That began to change in the second half of 2024, when market prices and exchange rates started climbing sharply. Even in rural areas, sellers have increasingly begun pricing goods in won based on that day’s exchange rate. As prices have failed to come down, farming communities have grown more anxious that holding onto won means watching the value of their assets erode.
“The exchange rate has kept rising for the past two years, while the value of the national currency (North Korean won) keeps falling,” the source said. “Even people in rural areas who used to have no interest in foreign currency now feel a strong need to convert even small amounts of money into it.”
The source continued, “Before COVID-19, $100 was worth about 800,000 to 900,000 North Korean won, but now it’s worth about 6 million won. Someone who had 900,000 won back then would only have the equivalent of about $15 today, while someone who had $100 now has 6 million won. That says it all.”
Won described as “worse than paper”
A source in Ryanggang province offered a similar account. “People in border areas use a lot of yuan, but in farming communities where trading isn’t the main livelihood, people tended to hold what little money they had in won,” the source said. “Over the past two years, though, prices and the exchange rate have risen enough to make people’s jaws drop, and it has become the topic of conversation everywhere. That’s made rural people feel it’s urgent to hold yuan too.”
Some in these communities have reportedly gone so far as to say the won “is now worth less than scrap paper” and that “only people who haven’t caught on still hold” it.
“Trust in the national currency was already low because of the currency reform (a reference to North Korea’s 2009 currency redenomination, which wiped out much of the population’s private savings), and it’s been shaken again by the recent surge in prices and the exchange rate,” the source said. “During the currency reform, everyone suffered losses equally. But now the gap between people widens sharply depending on whether they hold foreign currency, and that’s made the preference for it even more pronounced.”
The source added, “No matter how strictly the state cracks down on the use of foreign currency, what’s the point of a crackdown when the value of the national currency keeps falling like this? The reality now is that the belief that holding foreign currency, rather than won, is the only way to avoid losses is only getting stronger.”

items.title: Sinuiju flooding stalls North Korea-China cargo trade for days
items.summary: Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014. Cargo trucks traveling between […]
items.body_text:
Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014.
Cargo trucks traveling between Dandong in China’s Liaoning province and Sinuiju in North Korea’s North Pyongan province stopped running for more than two days starting Aug. 24, a source in North Korea told Daily NK on Friday.
“Trucks that had entered North Korea before Aug. 24 could not return to China, and new trucks could not enter either,” the source said. “There is talk that the cause was a problem in Sinuiju with processing, transporting or storing cargo.”
The exact cause of the suspension has not been officially confirmed, but Chinese trading circles believe it is likely directly linked to recent flooding in Sinuiju caused by heavy rain.
Daily NK previously reported that heavy rain in Sinuiju overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system, flooding low-lying areas and cutting off electricity and water supplies in some neighborhoods.
Local observers say the low-lying Apkang and Yokjon neighborhoods, which sit near the North Korea-China trade route, may also have seen roads and buildings flooded. Trade and vehicle traffic were likely halted temporarily to prevent further damage during the unloading, storage and transport of cargo, according to the assessment.
Investment mood turns cold
Notably, the incident is also weighing on investment sentiment toward Sinuiju, which had been rising in recent months.
“Businesspeople already knew Sinuiju was geographically vulnerable to flooding, but repeated flood damage like this inevitably changes their thinking,” the source said. “Just as things seemed to be going well, the uncontrollable variable of natural disaster resurfaced and threw cold water on the investment mood.”
The source added, “Many people had shown interest in the idea of developing the surrounding area into an international economic zone once the New Yalu River Bridge opens. But after this incident, there is a growing sense that there are problems that need to be resolved before questions like when the bridge will open or where to invest.”
Among Chinese businesspeople, a growing view holds that simply signing contracts with North Korea and building factories or warehouses is not enough to guarantee stability, and that North Korea must first upgrade its infrastructure to withstand flooding.
“There is growing concern that without protective construction work, such as raising the ground level with soil or rock fill and installing proper waterproofing and drainage systems, a single heavy rain could cause serious damage,” the source said. “Businesspeople have also grown more alert to natural disasters after seeing a string of sudden flood damage in border regions, including recent flooding in Nepal.”
The repeated flooding in Sinuiju is once again highlighting the city’s geographic limitations and weak infrastructure. As flood risk emerges as a major variable for Chinese businesspeople who had shown interest in investing in North Korea, attention is turning to what impact this will have on development around the New Yalu River Bridge, an area that had drawn attention amid expanding North Korea-China customs trade.
Reporting from inside North Korea
Daily NK operates networks of sources inside North Korea who document events in real-time and transmit information through secure channels. Unlike reporting based on state media, satellite imagery, or defector accounts from years past, our journalism comes directly from people currently living under the regime. We verify reports through multiple independent sources and cross-reference details before publication.
Our sources remain anonymous because contact with foreign media is treated as a capital offense in North Korea — discovery means imprisonmen

items.title: North Korea’s Sinuiju underwater again as drainage system fails
items.summary: Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has […]
items.body_text:
Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has become the latest sign of how fragile North Korea’s urban infrastructure remains against extreme weather.
According to a Daily NK source in North Pyongan province who spoke Thursday, heavy rain pounded the Sinuiju area on Aug. 23 and 24. The downpour briefly let up on Aug. 25 before picking up again overnight into Aug. 26.
“During the flooding in 2024, the river overflowed and that caused the damage. This time, the damage happened because the rainwater couldn’t drain away,” the source said. “The standing water can’t recede, and since it keeps raining, there’s even less chance for it to drain, so many areas remain flooded.”
“The rain stopped briefly on Aug. 25, and we thought the water might start receding, but it began raining again overnight into the early hours of Aug. 26,” the source added. “With the rain continuing like this, people don’t know when the water will finally recede, and they’re feeling anxious.”
The pattern of this flooding is markedly different from the 2024 disaster, according to the source. In 2024, the Yalu River overflowed and heavily damaged Wihwa Island and areas along the riverbank. This time, weak drainage conditions caused flooding across low-lying areas throughout the city.
In Sumun neighborhood, both electricity and water service remained cut off as of Aug. 26, and a significant number of single-story homes were submerged, forcing people to evacuate to higher ground. Temporary shelters have also been set up in some neighborhoods, including Ryonsang and Ryonha, to house flood victims as part of the response, according to the source.
Little state aid expected this time
Amid the damage, flood victims are reportedly resigned to the idea that nationwide recovery assistance will not follow this time, meaning they will have to rebuild their homes and belongings on their own once the water recedes.
“During the previous flooding, the Yalu River overflowed and the damage was highly visible from the outside, and the Marshal (Kim Jong Un) personally visited the area, so nationwide recovery assistance followed. This time, though, the visible damage isn’t as extensive,” the source said. “So there’s a strong sense among people that they shouldn’t expect much state support and will need to rebuild on their own.”
“In terms of the actual damage people have suffered, this time isn’t much different from before,” the source added. “With electricity and water cut off and homes and belongings submerged for days, people are struggling not only with immediate concerns like food and shelter, but even more with the uncertainty of how they’ll rebuild their lives once the water finally recedes.”
The latest flooding is seen as a case that exposes both the topographical characteristics of the Sinuiju area and its vulnerable drainage infrastructure. With North Korean authorities not disclosing detailed information about the damage this time, attention is turning to how extensive and thorough any future recovery efforts will be.
Rodong Sinmun reported Aug. 26 that rain and showers fell across most of the country between Aug. 23 and 24 due to a low-pressure trough and the seasonal rain front, with heavy rain also reported in several areas of North Pyongan province, some areas of South Pyongan province, and localized areas of Jagang province.
According to the newspaper, on Aug. 24 alone, Kusong received 408 millimeters of rain, Sinuiju 379 millimeters, Chonma 365 millimeters, Wihwa Island 329 millimeters, Uiju and Taechon 319 millimeters, Phihyon 267 millimeters, Nyongbyon 224 millimeters and Taegwan 216 millimeters, all considered extremely heavy rainfall. items.title: Live: Blues' resurgence continues with stirring wildcard win over Demons
items.summary: Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG. Follow live.
items.body_text:
Carlton defeats Melbourne to continue dream run with AFL wildcard round win
Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG.
Despite conceding the first four goals of the game, the Blues improved steadily throughout the game to grind the Demons down, before finally emerging 19-point winners.
Ben Ainsworth kicked three goals for Carlton, while Sam Walsh and rising star Jagga Smith were sensational in the midfield.
The Blues had multiple opportunities to put the game to bed in the last quarter, but it wasn't until Smith converted a set shot for his second of the evening when the result was put to bed.
Look back at how the action unfolded in the live blog below.

That's where we'll leave it
So that wraps up a heck of a weekend of footy for wildcard round.
The storylines are running wild and free, with Carlton going another week and a real test against Geelong at the MCG.
No Pies, and Scott Pendlebury going to the Suns - we haven't been short of surprises the last 48 hours!
We also say goodbye to a couple of players tonight, with the retirements of Jake Melksham and Tom McDonald for the Demons. Congratulations to both men on their careers.
We will be back on the blog on Thursday night for a mouthwatering qualifying final between Fremantle and Hawthorn at Perth Stadium (already a sell-out!).
But for now, this is Andrew McGarry saying thank you for joining us on tonight's blog and wishing you all a very good night!
Key Event
'It's the beginning of a journey for us': Demons coach Steven King reflects after season's end
Melbourne coach Steven King has been reflecting after the end of his first season as coach.
Speaking to the media he acknowledged that Carlton had played very well and that his team had not been able to take their chances.
He said he had spoken to a big room of players and staff after the game.
"It was a case of getting the balance right between the disappointment that goes with losing a final.
"It's the beginning of a journey that we're going on - we're not being defined by tonight.
"I couldn't be more proud of them for what they've done, their body of work.
"If you'd said at the start of the year that we'd go from seven wins to 15, I would have taken that any day of the week."
Asked about Kozzy Pickett, who had six shots at goal and scored 0.3, he replied:
"That probably sums up our night - we weren't able to pull through, it wasn't just (Pickett), we just didn't take our chances."
Key Event
Finals schedule confirmed
- Qualifying final: Thursday September 3, 8:10pm (AEST) - Fremantle vs Hawthorn (Perth Stadium)
- Elimination final: Friday September 4, 7:40pm (AEST) - Geelong vs Carlton (MCG)
- Qualifying final: Saturday September 5, 3:15pm (AEST) - Sydney vs Brisbane (SCG)
- Elimination final: Saturday September 5, 7:35pm (AEST) - Adelaide Crows vs Western Bulldogs (Adelaide Oval)
Match report: Blues stun Demons in wildcard to set up Cats final
Carlton have beaten Melbourne by 19 points in their AFL wildcard match to extend their fairytale resurgence into an elimination final clash with Geelong.
Under Josh Fraser, the Blues have famously fought back from a 1-8 start to the season that cost Michael Voss his job, to first make the wildcard round in 10th place, then reach the elimination final.
After fighting back from an early 21-point deficit, the Blues outgunned Melbourne, who finished seventh in the regular season, to claim a 10.14 (74) to 7.13 (55) victory in front of 91,733 fans at the MCG.
The Blues next face the sixth-placed Cats — who they beat by four points early in Fraser's initial caretaker coach tenure — at the MCG next Friday.
Adelaide will host the Western Bulldogs in Saturday's elimination final.

items.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
items.summary: South Sydney's Jai Arrow appears in the first of his final two matches for the Rabbitohs, leading the club out for their game against Gold Coast.
items.body_text:
Jai Arrow has led South Sydney out for their match against Gold Coast
Arrow was substituted in the opening seconds to a standing ovation.
What's next?
Arrow will do the same in next week's match against the Sydney Roosters to record his 100th NRL match.
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.
Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.
He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.
Loading Twitter content
Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.
The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.
He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.
Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.
It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.
Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.
"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.
"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."
The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.
The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.
Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.
Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.
AAP/ABC

items.title: Walker's season in jeopardy, Cowboys lock in top eight with Tigers win
items.summary: Roosters halfback Sam Walker will go for scans after sustaining a concerning ankle injury in his side's 26-12 loss to the Dolphins, while North Queensland lock in a finals spot with a 24-10 victory over Wests.
items.body_text:
Souths beat Titans after Jai Arrow tribute, Dolphins down Roosters, and Cowboys nab last NRL finals spot
An inspired defensive effort has seen the Dolphins hold on for a 26-12 victory over the Roosters, who lost star halfback Sam Walker to an ankle injury early in the second half.
Walker will go for scans for a suspected syndesmosis injury.
In Townsville, the Cowboys became the eighth and final team to lock in a finals berth with a 24-10 victory over Wests.
Earlier, South Sydney beat the Titans 42-22 to lock in a finals spot after a pre-game tribute to retiring Jai Arrow.
Loading...
Arrow, who was forced into retirement after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, started the game on the field before subbing off for Cameron Murray and will do the same next week to ensure he notches 100 games for the Rabbitohs.
In the NRLW, the Roosters have continued their winning start to the season with a 33-8 victory over Cronulla-Sutherland, the Titans downed the Raiders 26-20, and Newcastle defeated North Queensland 40-6.

items.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows
items.summary: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older peopleTaking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high chol
items.body_text:
Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.
Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.
People who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.
What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.
A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.
“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”
But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.
To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.
The researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.
The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.
In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.
Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.
“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.
“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”
The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.
Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”
Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.
Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.
