items.title: Plug-in solar panels could save households up to $370 a year – if Australia made them legal as in the UK
items.summary: A plug-in solar kit that costs about $1,000 ‘pays for itself in three years’, one expert saysGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastMillions of Australians could be saving up to $370 a year on energy bills and doing their bit for the climate crisis if Labor followed the UK’s lead in legalising plug-in solar panels, an advocacy group has said.Plug-in solar refers to small standalone solar units that could be attached to balconies or used in back yards and plugged into power po
items.body_text:
Millions of Australians could be saving up to $370 a year on energy bills and doing their bit for the climate crisis if Labor followed the UK’s lead in legalising plug-in solar panels, an advocacy group has said.
Plug-in solar refers to small standalone solar units that could be attached to balconies or used in back yards and plugged into power points, offsetting the energy used by household appliances.
Researchers have estimated Australians living in capital cities could save between $226 and $372 each year with a plug-in system.
While these systems are sold in Australia, they are not yet legal to plug in and use.
As a result, Heidi Lee Douglas, chief executive of Solar Citizens, said more than a third of Australians who rented or lived in apartments were missing out on the “bill-busting benefits” that solar homeowners enjoyed.
The campaign organisation has urged Australian governments to make plug-in solar available, after the technology was made legal in the United Kingdom this week, with units going on sale from Thursday.
“It’s unfair that more than three million Aussies who could benefit from portable plug-in solar panels are missing out because our regulations aren’t up to date with the latest technology,” she said.
“We see the UK, Germany, Spain and our neighbour New Zealand making plug-in solar available – so it’s time for Australian politicians and regulators to work it out here. If it’s good enough for the Kiwis and the Brits, it’s good enough for us.”
Solar and battery engineer Glen Morris, director of the Smart Energy Lab, said an 800-watt system could produce enough power to run a fridge, television and other appliances during the day.
“A kit that costs about $1,000 pays for itself in three years and keeps working for twenty,” he said. “For most renters it is the only form of solar they can own, and they take it with them when they move.”
Only about 11% of Australian renters have solar installed, compared with about 44% of homeowners, research by Energy Consumers Australia found. A similar gap existed for those living in apartments, with 6% having solar, compared with 39% of people in detached or semi-detached houses.
The consumer organisation said renters were missing out due to the “split incentive” problem, where landlords faced the upfront costs of installing solar, while tenants gained the most benefits. Apartment dwellers also faced structural barriers due to the complexities governing common property, the research found.
Along with unprecedented uptake of household solar and battery systems, the research revealed record quarterly investment in large-scale solar, with 1.8 gigawatts reaching final investment decision – the strongest result since the regulator began tracking investment activity.
The regulator’s acting chair, Carl Binning, said “the speed of the transition is accelerating”, adding that strong battery demand under the government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program had helped boost rooftop solar.
“We’ve now received more than 500,000 battery applications since the program started, which shows the scale of household demand when the economics stack up,” he said.

items.title: What we know about the Australians missing in the Nepal floods
items.summary: More than 40 Australians are among several thousand people unaccounted for after catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-Tibet borderHow the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastAn 11-year-old child, an ADF member and many other pilgrims and trekkers have been named among the Australians missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border.As of Saturday there were 41 Australia
items.body_text:
1. Himalayan Glacier Adventures group
Fifteen of the missing Australians were on a pilgrimage with the Himalayan Glacier tour group to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and the Bon faith. All but one in the group are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community.
Among those unaccounted for are NSW couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, as well as Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20. The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook cricket club in Sydney’s north-west.
“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.
“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”
Also in the group is a family of four: Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11. Shylaja’s sister, Vaishnavi, said she had lost contact with the family on the morning of the flood as the family prepared to cross an immigration checkpoint at the Tibet-Nepal border.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said. “Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family.”
Sagar Pandey, founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people.
Pandey said on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area where the group was staying and had little hope they survived.
4. Isha Foundation
A group of 11 Australians remain missing after travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage.
The foundation confirmed that 11 Australians among a group of 80 missing pilgrims, were inside an immigration building at the Gyirong border crossing when the flood hit.
Among them, Guardian Australia has confirmed, is missing Australian woman Sumi Adhikari. Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal seeking information about her whereabouts.
“We still have no clear or official information about Sumi or the other members of her group,” Pandey said on Saturday morning.
Also missing is 42-year-old Australian man Bharat Mangwani, who was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning. He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” close friend Kushagra Tiwari said. Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has travelled to Nepal to search.

items.title: As insults fly around trade, negotiators for Canada and the U.S. avoid getting personal in public
items.summary: Politicians from Canada and the United States have thrown varying degrees of personal insults back and forth across the border this week, but the two governments' trade negotiators avoided getting personal — at least in public. Experts believe the two trade leads are striking a different tone because they have a different role to play as the dispute heats up.
items.body_text:
As insults fly around trade, negotiators for Canada and the U.S. avoid getting personal in public
Politicial scientists, PR expert say negotiators are staying out of the fray as part of wider strategy
This week, politicians from Canada and the United States have traded personal insults across the border, describing others as weak, nasty, foolish, ridiculous and a loser — the last paired with a curt invitation to "kiss my ass."
The taunts have escalated the feud between the two countries, which has already led to crushing tariffs on tens of billions of dollars worth of cross-border goods. But the two governments' trade negotiators have avoided getting personal, at least in public.
Political scientists and a public relations expert say the trade leads are striking a different tone because, like their predecessors in past negotiations, their bosses have given them a specific role to play in the trade dispute — one that would only be made harder by bad blood.
"What we're seeing is a choreography, a play, if you like, where you've got different people playing different roles to have the overall effect that you want to achieve," said Jaime Watt, founder of the public relations firm Navigator.
Negotiators don't help themselves with 'silly insults': professor
Trade talks between the U.S. and Canada collapsed on Aug. 21, with each side later blaming the other for spoiling what seemed to be the closest chance at a deal in months.
Neither government has released the text of the scuttled agreement, and negotiators have mostly cited confidentiality when pressed for details, leaving the public to rely largely on politicians' comments to gauge progress — or the lack of it.
On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump further antagonized Canadians when he directed his government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move quickly dismissed up north as unnecessarily provocative and insulting. He had previously referred to Canadian officials as "clowns" and described Ontario's premier as the "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother.
In separate interviews with CBC News, the two countries' respective cabinet members took a different tack. They criticized the other governments' economic policies but didn't make it personal.
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said he didn't want spend time dwelling on "who said what about whom" and described his dealings with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer as "always personal and professional."
Two days later, Greer sidestepped a question whether his boss' rhetoric complicates his job.
"I would just say my job is quite narrow, and on trade relations, it's quite narrow," Greer told CBC News on Wednesday, describing his relationship with LeBlanc as "good."
"It's about economics."
Experts said the trade leads are likely avoiding personal insults in public because poisoning the well won't help them achieve their objective: securing the best deal possible for their respective countries.
"They're not going to launch silly insults against one another because it's not good for actually productive conversations," said Aaron Ettinger, a political science professor at Carleton University. "If they can't stand each other, then it's going to be hard to be in the same room with one another."
Away from the negotiating table, political leaders have their own goals.
"They're the highest ranking politicians in either jurisdiction and they're both using their space to try to convince people of something," said Lori Turnbull, a political science professor at Dalhousie University.
In a departure from his typical conciliatory tone, Carney used the language of sovereignty and war on Saturday as he called for a generational shift away from an unreliable adversary.
Turnbull, Ettinger and Watt agreed the prime minister was looking to rally Canadians and project strength to global allies as the country enters a costly economic war with the U.S.

items.title: Russian attack on Kyiv region kills at least 37
items.summary: At least 27 people have been killed following a Russian attack on the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, officials said Saturday.
items.body_text:
Russian attack on Kyiv region kills at least 37
Almost constant air raids in Ukrainian capital have now reached their 3rd day
At least 37 people have been killed following a Russian attack on the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, officials said Saturday.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the local regional military administration, said at least 50 residential buildings had been damaged in the attack, which also sparked a large-scale fire that spread to homes and a restaurant.
In a statement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a warehouse had been struck in the village of Myla "followed by a detonation."
He did not give details on the site but wrote that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence.
"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader wrote that a care home for elderly people and people with disabilities and residential buildings were damaged.
- VideoRussian attacks kill at least 20 in Kyiv
- Russian missile and drone barrage in Ukrainian capital region kills 17
"More than 370 people have already been evacuated, and the evacuation is ongoing," he said.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi also didn't offer information on the warehouse targeted. He referred to an attack on the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve earlier in the month, which hit an ammunition depot, killing 22, and triggered large detonations and fires that tore through nearby homes.
"Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson," Koretskyi said. "In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again."
In a statement, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said that it had attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics centre and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.
Almost constant air raids in Kyiv have now reached their third day, choking the economy in the Ukrainian capital and severely disrupting civilian life more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of its neighbour.
Elsewhere, Russian attacks across Ukraine's southern Kherson region on Saturday killed two people and wounded 27, a local official said.
Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the region administration, said attacks had damaged homes and apartment blocks and that one child was among the injured.
Earlier in the week, Prokudin said Russia has intensified attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, which is about 70 per cent under Russian control. He also urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions because of the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter.
Meanwhile, three people have been killed and nine injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia's Belgorod region, local authorities said on their Telegram channel.
Three of the injured are in serious condition, authorities said.
With files from Reuters

items.title: Nepal flash flood death toll climbs to 579, with 32 Canadians, permanent residents among missing
items.summary: Thirty-two Canadian citizens and permanent residents are among the nearly 2,000 people missing after the catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand confirmed Friday.
items.body_text:
Nepal flash flood death toll climbs to 579, with 32 Canadians, permanent residents among missing
Authorities warn that a newly formed, overflowing lake could trigger further flooding
Thirty-two Canadian citizens and permanent residents are among the nearly 2,000 people missing after the catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand confirmed Friday.
Anand confirmed during a media conference that 579 bodies had been recovered in the area so far and 1,924 people were still unaccounted for. Of those, 517 are foreign nationals, she said.
No Canadians are among those confirmed dead, Anand added.
"Nepal is facing a devastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage," she said.
Canada also announced it was providing $5 million to support emergency relief funds to Nepal.
Meanwhile, rescuers worked through mud and debris Friday in areas devastated by the flood, continuing the search for those still missing.
Nepalese and Chinese authorities also warned of further flooding from a lake that formed upstream after Wednesday's disaster and was already overflowing. They urged people in potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says 3,742 people have been rescued.
The missing include tourists from several countries. Nepalese army spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press that a team had been deployed Friday to the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project near the Nepal-China border following reports that people were trapped inside a tunnel.
"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."
The rescue effort has been challenging, and it's difficult to access some of the communities that have been most affected, Santosh Pandey, Oxfam's humanitarian lead in Nepal, told CBC's As it Happens from Kathmandu.
"Entire villages, entire communities, have been swept away. There is no one actually in the community to help each other," Pandey said.
"A lot of public infrastructure has been damaged, a lot of hospitals and health facilities have been completely swept away.
"It's a very chaotic situation right now."
'We have to find him'
As rescuers work to reach remaining survivors, desperate families have crowded around hospitals trying to see if their loved ones can be identified among the hundreds of bodies that have been recovered.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, relatives peer at grim images lining a wall outside the forensic identification unit.
The photos show the badly battered bodies of victims, including young children who had been pulled from the mud.
“I came here because I hope I find [my brother]. I will search until my last breath is gone,” said Nirmala Sapkota Koholi, 49, who lives in the city of Lalitpur, south of Kathmandu.
“I have to go everywhere, we have to find him.”
Koholi told CBC News that her younger brother, Pradip Kumar Sapkota, was working as a driver with a group of pilgrims, including some from the United States and India. He had been on his phone with his daughter at 8:45 a.m. Wednesday. His daughter heard a loud boom and then the call suddenly cut off. They haven’t been able to reach him since.
Koholi has been to three hospitals and believes one of the victim photos could be her brother.
“He was a very good person. That is why God took him away.”
Red Cross raises alarm about secondary flood
Red Cross officials, at a news conference in Switzerland, expressed concern about a secondary flood and said that the organization's rescue operations were temporarily halted after trucks with relief supplies were were blocked by further flooding.
"We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need," said David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Soci

items.title: Tens of thousands mourn King Harald V in Norway as his son takes the throne
items.summary: Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as king either later Saturday or in the coming days
items.body_text:
Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects to Norway’s King Harald V on Saturday, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo a day after the monarch died at 89.
A sea of colourful flowers covered Slottsplassen, the square in front of the palace, as a steady stream of Norwegians filed past. A palace gardener removed some bouquets on the south side of the palace to keep pathways clear, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Palace workers also collected cards soaked after a nightly downpour and dried them to preserve the mourners’ messages for posterity, NRK reported.
Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially on Saturday so people could light candles, write down their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books.
The coffin arrived at the royal palace Friday evening from the National Hospital in Oslo where Harald died.
“It’s special, intimate, and lovely. I’m placing my right hand on my chest in gratitude to him and the royal family,” Roni Ervik, 46, told NRK as he paid his respects. He said he was also paying tribute to the late king on behalf of his family, who are from western Norway.
Harald V died Friday morning and his 53-year-old son, Crown Prince Haakon, became King Haakon VIII.
Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne.
Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, he stepped in as the country’s regent on several occasions.
Later Saturday, a choir was expected to sing in the Royal Palace Square. The new king was also scheduled to hold audiences with the speaker of Norway’s parliament, the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra also expected to attend, NRK reported.
Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as king either later Saturday or in the coming days.
His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction.
A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported.
Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

items.title: Survivors return to Nepal villages devastated by floods as families await news of nearly 3,000 missing
items.summary: Death toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 633 dead and at least 32 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing
items.body_text:
Most arrive with nothing except the clothes they are wearing.
As rescue efforts in communities buried by catastrophic flash floods along the border between Nepal and China entered their fourth day Saturday, authorities continued finding survivors and transporting them to safety. At relief centres, as some arrive, families wait anxiously for news of their loved ones as the death toll and the number of people unaccounted for continued to rise.
After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 633 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing.
The Globe and Mail reported that on Friday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said at least 32 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing.
Canada sent five consular officials who have arrived in the region to support Canadians, Ms. Anand said. “We are ready to send more officials as required,” she said.
In Nuwakot, one of the Nepali districts devastated by the floods, helicopters resumed operations before noon Saturday after poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue activities.
Some helicopters were loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice. Others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors.
Religious pilgrims from Canada at building swept away in Tibet-Nepal border floods
An older man was carefully helped off one helicopter, while a soldier carried an older woman on his back to a medical tent. There, medics checked her blood pressure, breathing and heartbeat, as well as her teeth and gums.
About a dozen people emerged from another helicopter. Soldiers carried several babies who had been evacuated.
The evacuees had been brought from the nearby community of Trishuli.
Villagers return to devastated homes
As people were still leaving Trishuli, some village residents were returning to see what could be salvaged from their decimated homes.
One boy walked out of the village carrying muddy sandals from his house. Another woman, Shoba Shretha, returned to find her dog, Sweetie, who she was forced to leave behind when the floods came. Shretha sat on the ground petting her and feeding her water from a bottle.
At some point, relief coordinators cleared villagers, reporters and volunteers from the entrance to Trishuli, as excavation equipment drove into the flooded village to dig.
Families begin to lose hope
In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning, desperately searching for news of missing loved ones.
Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital notice board, clutching photographs and scanning injured patients’ lists in the hope of finding them.
Dil Maya Lama stood weeping outside the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her missing 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had travelled from Ramechhap, about 130 kilometres away.
“I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she said. “There is no information about him.”
Nelza Moktan anxiously sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa.
“I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said.
Families covered hospital walls with posters showing missing relatives, photographs and contact numbers in a desperate appeal for any clue that could bring them home.
Nearby were photographs of unidentified bodies which officials put up in hopes they could be recognized by families or friends.
Gajendra Rawat, a security official at the hospital help desk, said families had so far registered around 1,600 missing persons since the disaster struck. “People are coming from all parts of Nepal,” he said.
Families search paper lists for any clues
Back in Nuwakot, military personnel taped sheets of paper listing dozens of missing people to a wall at a relief centre, prompting families to crowd around them.

items.title: Russian strike near Kyiv triggers explosion, killing 37 as Zelensky vows punishment
items.summary: In one of the deadliest attacks on Ukraine this year, at least 50 residential buildings were damaged
items.body_text:
At least 37 people have been killed following a Russian strike close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, officials said Saturday, one of the deadliest attacks to hit Ukraine this year.
The attack sparked a fire in the Bucha district, west of Kyiv, that swept through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the local regional military administration.
Kyiv investigates warehouse targeted in attack
In a statement on the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a warehouse had been struck in the village of Myla, “followed by a detonation.”
He did not give details on the site, but wrote in the same message that Ukrainian law forbade the storage of ammunition close to civilian homes and that criminal proceedings had been opened.
“Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” Zelensky said.

The Ukrainian leader also wrote that a care home for elderly people and people with disabilities had been damaged, and that an evacuation from the area was ongoing.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi also didn’t offer information on the warehouse targeted, but referenced an attack on the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve early in July, which hit an ammunition depot, killing 22 and triggering large detonations and fires that tore through nearby homes.
“Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.”
In a statement, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said that it had attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics center and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.
Zelenskyy later announced that two officials from state-owned companies, including Ukraine’s largest arms producer, Ukroboronprom, had illegally allowed the storage of weapons on the site in Vyshneve and would be held accountable.
Russia bombards Kyiv with third day of nearly non-stop attacks
Three days of almost constant Russian air raids on Kyiv have choked the economy in the Ukrainian capital and severely disrupted civilian life more than 4 1/2 years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
Russian strikes on the southern Kherson region Saturday killed two people and wounded 27 more, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the region administration, said in a statement on social media.
He said that attacks had damaged homes and apartment blocks, and that one child was among the injured.
Earlier in the week, Prokudin said that Russia has intensified attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, which is about 70% under Russian control. He also urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions because of the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter.
Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered drones, and their numbers will keep growing as Moscow sees their effectiveness, said Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, in comments to journalists Friday that were embargoed until Saturday.
“Means of attack always outpace means of defense. We will certainly need to adapt. It will take time,” Palisa said. He said interceptor drones currently available to Ukraine, which could theoretically intercept jet-powered drones, are not yet to demonstrate the expected effectiveness, though Ukraine is working on solutions.

items.title: Does a clear freezie taste as sweet? The foods going colourless because ‘it’s better for you’
items.summary: From pale yellow nacho chips to freezies that look like ice, some food companies are dropping cosmetic colourings completely
items.body_text:
Does a clear freezie taste as sweet? The foods going colourless because 'it's better for you'
From pale yellow nacho chips to freezies that look like ice, some food companies are dropping cosmetic colourings completely
Do grape-flavoured freezies need to be purple? And must the nacho cheese dust left on your fingertips be quite so flaming orange? Some food and beverage companies are betting not, dropping the colourings altogether in a bid to remove artificial food dyes.
As consumers’ priorities shift and regulatory scrutiny rises in the United States, the food and beverage industry is moving away from synthetic dyes. According to a March 2026 survey from Consumer Reports, roughly 72 per cent of adults are at least somewhat concerned about the use of artificial food dyes, which research has linked to health issues including allergies and hyperactivity.
Synthetic food dyes serve a purely cosmetic purpose, and eliminating them is a step in the right direction, experts told National Post. Swapping synthetic food dyes for natural ones is proving challenging for the food and beverage industry. Natural tints made from algae, minerals and plants can be costly and less shelf-stable, causing some companies to move in a different, tintless direction.
PepsiCo Inc. went “completely colourless” last year with its Simply NKD line of Cheetos and Doritos, reformulated without artificial flavours or dyes. Promising the “same intensity,” the new products generated US$3 million in sales in their first month in stores, RTI International told Food Dive, citing Circana data. Other companies are following. Jel Sert, the maker of Otter Pops, Fla-Vor-Ice and Kool Pops, for instance, reportedly plans to remove all colourings from its treats by early 2028. Colourless Otter Pops made with apple juice concentrate are already on the market.
Matt Ingemi, Jel Sert’s chief strategy officer, told Bloomberg that given the challenges of natural dyes, the company will drop tints altogether and use colourful images on packaging to convey flavour. “We’ll make it fun.”
Yu Ma, a professor of marketing at McGill University, says this approach makes sense in a crowded retail environment, where brands want to stand out as much as possible from the competition. “Without colour, you’re losing that punch in attracting people’s attention, and they don’t want to lose that,” says Ma.

- Advertisement 1Story continues below
Consumer acceptance of colourless foods and drinks depends on the type of product, says David Soberman, a professor of marketing and the Canadian National Chair of Strategic Marketing at the University of Toronto. For foods such as freezies, which tend to be consumed directly from the casing, leaning into vibrant packaging “is very effective” at getting around the issue of a colourless product. “The more steps there are between taking the product out of the package and consumption, the less effective it is.”
Something like pop, on the other hand, that’s drunk straight from the can or bottle but also dispensed from soda fountains and served at restaurants and bars, risks losing its identity along with its distinctive hue. “Each context is different, and so you can actually assess the challenge that the marketer has based on the actual steps that a person goes through to consume the product,” says Soberman.
In our health-conscious era, consumers might link bright colours with ultra-processed foods, and avoid them as a result, adds Ma. Colourless products could be considered “more natural” or “better for you.” Attitudes were different in 1992, when Crystal Pepsi hit store shelves. Ma discusses the clear cola in his marketing class as “a classic example of a new product failure.” It was gone by the end of 1994. “I feel like there is a much better chance for a product like Crystal Pepsi to succeed today than 30 years ago.”

items.title: Raymond J. de Souza: Trump’s America is losing its grip
items.summary: As in the now-famous photos of a bald eagle attacking a Canada goose, the U.S. is failing to conquer its targets
items.body_text:
Raymond J. de Souza: Trump's America is losing its grip
As in the now-famous photos of a bald eagle attacking a Canada goose, the U.S. is failing to conquer its targets
The White House posted to social media an image of a bald eagle attacking a Canada goose on a frozen Lake Ontario, taken by Burlington, Ont. photographer Mervyn Sequeira. It turned out the photo was one in a series that showed the goose suffered but survived, and the eagle flew away, defeated and hungry.
It’s not entirely a surprise that the White House propaganda arm would be misrepresenting what happened. It is distressing that the accurate term now for White House communications is propaganda. President Donald Trump, after all, chose the same name for his social media platform, “Truth,” as the Soviet communist party did for its daily newspaper, “Pravda.” In its day, Pravda was more egregious but less embarrassing.
In general, I have little affection for our official national animal, the beaver, and active dislike for the Canada goose. An airborne wedge is majestic, but a gaggle at ground is a defecating menace. It seems to me a lack of imagination on the part of Prime Minister Mark Carney that he has not (yet?) unleashed the geese to befoul the lawns at Mar-a-Lago. The Canada goose would be at home there; it is only fitting that an excess of excrement be deposited in a place from which so much of it is sent abroad.
Failing that, at least Carney could rename Branta canadensis the Trump Goose. The president might even consider it a compliment. Trading Trump Goose for Lake America would be a big, beautiful deal if the flocks stayed permanently in Florida.
As national symbols go, I prefer the moose, to which I expect a bald eagle would give a wide berth. It is an insult to the glorious bald eagle to identify it with the Trump administration, but the Russian bear has had to suffer association with the Kremlin in times past, and now again.
As Pravda Trump will not tell you, most North American bald eagles are now Canadian, the Americans having neglected to properly manage their own. Should a convocation of same fly south, it is not clear whether the Canadian ones would face a tariff at the border, or deportation upon roosting.
That bald eagles are more likely Canadian than American tells us something about this declining American moment. Consider the following items from the past fortnight.
The Trump administration declared economically lethal sanctions against Iran. This is supposedly an augmentation of the “crippling” and “maximum” sanctions American administrations have been applying for decades. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Iranian banks in the UAE had to close immediately. They remained fully open for business.
No one country can entirely sanction another without allies, and America has fewer of those than a year ago. Trump’s economic strangulation of Iran will depend principally upon the UAE and China, and to a lesser degree upon India, Russia and Turkey.
The eagle and goose on Lake Ontario is good image for the entire Iranian fiasco. The American-Israeli operation swooped in with fearsome air power. But on the ground, the goose — peacock in the Iranian context — kept control of the (frozen) waters.
Everyone is now talking about asymmetric warfare; the weaker power may not prevail but can frustrate and inflict real damage on the stronger power with drones, radar-evading missiles and the like. It’s foolish to wrestle with a Russian bear, but the bear may indeed be helpless against the drone that flies up behind it.
The eagle has talons, but the goose has bowels. Which bird causes more damage to more people?
Canadians felt proud when our government refused to capitulate to the Trump administration, which desires capitulation and conquest more than it does mutual co-operation with allies or even the common good of the American people. items.title: Economists have some ideas about how to Trump-proof the economy
items.summary: The most powerful policy play, they say, would be an overhaul of Canada's tax system
items.body_text:
Economists have some ideas about how to Trump-proof the economy
The most powerful policy play, they say, would be an overhaul of Canada's tax system
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is under attack, bombarded by U.S. tariffs and a trade partner that moves goalposts on a whim.
The federal government’s initial response was to offer short-term support payments for companies and workers hit by this latest round of American tariffs.
But economists say it’s the long-term policy moves that will do much more to inoculate the Canadian economy against the Trump tariffs, not to mention fuel a higher national standard of living.
The most powerful policy play, they say, would be an overhaul of Canada’s tax system because that could improve national competitiveness, something that was sorely needed even without the Trump tariff threat. They argue that tax changes, specifically cuts to personal and corporate income, would encourage increased investment and exports, which would then fuel increased economic growth.
“Canada really needs to do something large on tax reform,” said Jack Mintz, the president’s fellow at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy. “I think it’s even more crucial today.”
While Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has yet to signal the government’s broad goals for its upcoming budget this fall, the stars may have aligned for big change. The trade rupture has given Ottawa and the provinces rare political cover to make moves that might have been unpopular during normal times. The Liberals are also led by an economist, have a majority and are likely at least a couple of years from the next election.
The Liberal government might be leaning that way. Even before the trade war with the U.S., the party had vowed to hold a review of the corporate tax system during last year’s federal election campaign, although that promise that has not yet been kept.
The question is whether the Carney government will seize this moment to boost the economy or defy Winston Churchill’s quip to “never let a good crisis go to waste.”
It’s not just economists feeling the tides of change. The leaders of two of Canada’s largest banks, Scott Thomson of the Bank of Nova Scotia and Darryl White of the Bank of Montreal, said Tuesday that the tariff fight should trigger the federal government to act.
“There is an opportunity for the Canadian federal and provincial governments to recognize the moment for what it is and use it to drive transformational policy change,” White told equity analysts, “and not let this moment go to waste.”
A handful of economists surveyed by National Post were largely consistent in what they’d like to see the government do to spur and Trump-proof the economy.
Each said that their recipes for growth include, and usually begin with, income tax cuts: both corporate and personal.
Tim Sargent, director of economic growth and prosperity at University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy, said these two taxes touch and influence virtually every inch of the economy, which means that reducing them would also mean widespread improvements to competitiveness.
Fatter wallets
Despite some tepid cuts to personal income taxes in recent decades, economists say Canadians still pay way too much and the problem has been getting worse. Canada now relies more on personal income taxes for its revenue than any other G7 country.
While governments’ slice from Canadians’ pay cheques has been climbing for decades, Mintz pointed out that personal income taxes accounted for 11 per cent of GDP in 2010, but grew to 13 per cent by 2023. Personal income taxes are now responsible for easily the biggest chunk of government revenue, and almost twice the amount of any other form of federal or provincial tax.
While governments need money to pay for health care, education, defence and other big spending items, economists say it’s critical that legislators take the minimum and in a way that is as harmless as possible.

items.title: «24 poses (portraits)»: une véritable affaire de famille
items.summary: Vingt-sept ans après sa création, la pièce de Serge Boucher est mise en scène chez Duceppe par Édith Patenaude.
items.body_text:
Créée en 1999, 24 poses (portraits) était la troisième pièce de Serge Boucher, après Natures mortes (1993) et Motel Hélène (1997). Pour l’auteur de 36 ans, il s’agissait d’un premier grand plateau, d’une première pièce à plusieurs personnages et d’un premier grand succès populaire. Parmi les huit comédiens dirigés alors au Centre du Théâtre d’Aujourd’hui par René Richard Cyr, on trouvait Guylaine Tremblay dans le rôle de la jeune Carole. Vingt-sept ans plus tard, la comédienne s’apprête à incarner Claire, la mère de Carole, dans un spectacle mis en scène chez Duceppe par Édith Patenaude.
« Au moment de la création, explique l’auteur, je me souviens d’avoir pensé que si la pièce était remontée un jour, il faudrait que le rôle de la mère soit interprété par Guylaine. Ça m’apparaissait comme une évidence. » Effectivement, dans cette dramaturgie qui découle en quelque sorte de celles de Michel Tremblay et de Claude Meunier, mais en adoptant un hyperréalisme plus radical, moins métaphorique, moins satirique, la comédienne se meut comme un poisson dans l’eau. « C’est une grande chance de pouvoir plonger à nouveau dans cette pièce qui, à mon avis, n’a pas vieilli d’une seconde. Tous les personnages sont extraordinaires. Ils ont des défauts, bien sûr, mais on ne peut pas ne pas les aimer. »
« Écrire 24 poses, se souvient Boucher, c’était l’occasion de rompre avec les pièces à plusieurs courts tableaux que j’avais faites auparavant. C’était le moment d’écrire une pièce en trois actes, une fresque familiale d’inspiration tchékhovienne dans laquelle il ne se passerait absolument rien, sinon une affaire à la toute fin. Pour une fois, je me suis dit : arrête de tourner autour du pot et parle de ta famille ! Ces personnages, ils correspondent à des archétypes, bien sûr, mais c’est aussi ce que j’appelle du vrai monde. »
Quelle famille !
L’action de 24 poses se déroule le dimanche 10 août 1997, dans la cour arrière d’un bungalow de Charlesbourg, en banlieue de Québec. Ce jour-là, où la comédienne Marie-Soleil Tougas va trouver la mort dans un accident d’avion, le clan Dubé se réunit pour célébrer les 40 ans de Richard (Marc Beaupré), le fils aîné de Claire (Guylaine Tremblay) et Denis (Martin Drainville). Sont aussi de la partie Nicole (Myriam Fournier), la conjointe de Richard, Carole (Émilie Bibeau), la sœur de Richard, André (Benoit Mauffette), le conjoint de Carole, sans oublier mononcle Roger (Frédéric Blanchette), le frère de Claire, et François (Gabriel Favreau), le frère de Carole et de Richard, le benjamin, sorte de mouton noir de la famille, celui qui vit à Montréal et qui « écrit ».
                                
                    « Des répliques semblables à celles de 24 poses, j’en entends dans mes soupers de famille, il m’arrive même d’en prononcer moi-même. »
Guylaine Tremblay
Photo: Marie-France Coallier / Le Devoir
La famille, ici comme ailleurs, c’est un territoire miné sur lequel on n’a pour ainsi dire pas le choix de s’avancer. La famille, c’est une galerie de personnages qui parlent beaucoup pour dire peu, ou alors rien du tout, des gens qu’on a souvent autant de raison d’aimer que de détester. La famille, c’est un engagement qu’on respecte… pour le meilleur et pour le pire. Impossible, en assistant à 24 poses, de ne pas penser à notre propre famille, de ne pas remettre en question la nature de nos liens. On rigole, on grince des dents, mais on procède aussi, nécessairement, à une forme d’introspection.
« Je pose sur toute cette famille un regard plein de tendresse, explique Guylaine Tremblay. Des répliques semblables à celles de 24 poses, j’en entends dans mes soupers de famille, il m’arrive même d’en prononcer moi-même. Parler de la météo, balancer des banalités, accrocher sur des détails, c’est une façon d’entrer en dialogue, un moyen de faire comprendre aux autres qu’on tient à eux. items.title: «Chambres noires»: entre l’ombre et la lumière
items.summary: Suivant les traces de la photographe américaine Vivian Maier, Dominique Fortier raconte son histoire «la plus fragile».
items.body_text:
En 2007, dans une vente aux enchères de Chicago, John Maloof, un jeune Américain, a fait l’acquisition un peu à l’aveugle de boîtes pleines de négatifs, de rouleaux de pellicule jamais développés, de bobines de film et d’impressions photographiques. Un univers englouti reprenait vie.
Cette photographe de rue amatrice, une parfaite inconnue qui a travaillé pendant 40 ans comme nounou, s’appelait Vivian Maier (1926-2009). L’existence de cette femme, révélée au monde grâce au fascinant documentaire réalisé par John Maloof et Charlie Siskel en 2013, Finding Vivian Maier (À la recherche de Vivian Maier), se résume aujourd’hui à peu de choses, sinon aux dizaines de milliers de photographies qu’elle a prises — beaucoup d’autoportraits, Rolleiflex autour du cou —, dont certaines sont exposées aujourd’hui dans plusieurs musées dans le monde.
Une sorte de mystère, un mythe, dont Dominique Fortier s’intéresse à l’« œuvre fantôme, inachevée et sauvage » dans Chambres noires, son onzième titre en solo. Un livre dans lequel elle mêle des jalons de l’histoire de la photographie, des hypothèses sur la vie de Vivian Maier ainsi que des éléments pour elle plus intimes, qui tourne autour du motif de la révélation — qui consiste, en photographie argentique, à rendre visible l’image latente et invisible enregistrée sur le film ou le papier lors de l’exposition à la lumière.
                                
                    « L’œil est toujours entraîné vers on ne sait pas quoi. C’est comme s’il voulait s’échapper du cadre. »
Dominique Fortier
Photo: Valérian Mazataud Le Devoir
Écrivaine discrète, Dominique Fortier semble s’y dévoiler un peu plus qu’à l’habitude, évoquant en parallèle de la vie de Vivian Maier l’existence de sa sœur aînée décédée lorsqu’elle avait 3 ans. Un « petit fantôme » qui l’accompagne depuis et dont elle n’a conservé aucun souvenir. Sinon des photos de famille charcutées, une tristesse diffuse, un silence qui pèse. La présence d’une absence. « Les secrets, les silences. Tous ces blancs qui font aussi les livres. »
Une histoire, écrit l’autrice d’Au péril de la mer (Alto, 2015, Prix littéraire du Gouverneur général), née à Québec en 1972, qui est pour elle « la plus personnelle et la plus fragile ». Et c’est armée de sa pudeur coutumière qu’elle développe dans Chambres noires son intérêt pour les fantômes.
« Son œuvre est caractérisée par une chose que j’appellerais l’esthétique du choc, de la collision. Elle fonctionne en mettant ensemble des choses qui ne devraient pas se rencontrer », fait remarquer Dominique Fortier depuis sa maison du Maine, en cette fin du mois d’août qui marque à regret le début du compte à rebours des jours qu’il lui reste avant de rentrer à Montréal. Dans les photos de Vivian Maier, témoin autant d’une époque que d’un lieu, « l’œil est toujours entraîné vers on ne sait pas quoi. C’est comme s’il voulait s’échapper du cadre ». Son regard lui semble aussi porter un mélange de tendresse et de quelque chose d’implacable.
La petite-fille d’Emily Dickinson
Si l’écrivaine ne se souvient pas de sa première rencontre avec Vivian Maier et avec son œuvre, elle a l’impression que c’est comme si elles avaient toujours été là. Mais elle se souvient que le 11 août 2025, en rentrant à Montréal après avoir passé l’été au bord de la mer, Dominique Fortier a aperçu dans la vitrine d’une maison de la presse la couverture d’un magazine, un numéro spécial, consacré à la photographe américaine. « Je ne sais pas ce que ça a provoqué chez moi, mais c’était suffisamment fort pour que j’achète la revue, que je rentre chez nous, que je la pose à côté de moi, puis que je me mette à écrire tout de suite. Il y avait quelque chose comme un appel. » Ces photos lui parlaient, elles ont réveillé en elle quelque chose.
C’était un peu, relate-t-elle, comme si Vivian Maier lui disait : « Raconte ma vie. » Alors que c’était peut-être elle, en réalité, qui aidait Dominique Fortier à raconter la sienne. Quelques mois plus tard, en novemb

items.title: Le plafond magique du Musée d’art contemporain des Laurentides
items.summary: Il faut lever les yeux avec une «black light» pour que se révèle l’attrait le plus original du MAC LAU.
items.body_text:
Création emblématique, chef-d’œuvre méconnu ou artefact chouchou : cette série présente chaque fois une pièce de collection soigneusement choisie pour incarner un courant, une époque ou la simple raison d’être d’un musée.
Le petit Musée d’art contemporain des Laurentides (MAC LAU) est un peu caché. Sis discrètement au deuxième étage du vieux palais de justice de Saint-Jérôme, coincé au centre d’un vertical sandwich entre la bibliothèque et les locaux de l’organisme Histoire et archives Laurentides, on peut passer devant sans le voir. Comme on peut rater son attrait le plus original : sa collection suspendue, cachée au-dessus de toutes les têtes…
À la billetterie, en vous accueillant, il arrive qu’on vous remette… une lampe de poche. Pourtant, des néons émane l’habituelle lumière bleue des lieux publics. Mais si vous allumez votre lampe de poche…
… et que vous levez les yeux au ciel dans la petite pièce principale du musée, vous verrez apparaître sous le faisceau en traits bleu mauve un personnage mirifique, des formes, des lettres, quelques bêtes, qui ornent comme à l’encre invisible les très ordinaires tuiles à plafond suspendu, et ne se révèlent que sous l’éclat de black light.
Votre journaliste s’est retrouvée couchée sur le dos au beau milieu du plancher, pour mieux observer les dessins de 29 artistes, dont Karen Tam, Bonnie Baxter, André Fournelle, Rober Racine, la Famille Plouffe et Peter Gnass.
« Il y en a partout dans la salle », explique la conservatrice et codirectrice par intérim Elizabeth Lauzon. Le projet a produit une exposition en 2020, Quand la collection prédit l’avenir.
Critique très créative
« Quand, comme musée, on acquiert des tuiles du plafond et on le travaille comme espace d’exposition, c’est parce qu’on manque d’espace… », sourit Mme Lauzon. Le MAC LAU fait 2000 pieds carrés.
Le geste, muséalement créatif et très joueur, est « un peu une critique institutionnelle qu’on a gentiment faite au ministère de la Culture ».
En effet, dans les critères de financement de cette époque, un musée qui possédait une collection de plus de 1000 œuvres obtenait plus de points, et donc plus de chances d’avoir un financement au supérieur. Un musée qui en avait 5000 avait encore un point de plus. « C’est purement quantitatif », estime la conservatrice.
Le MAC LAU comptait alors 800 œuvres, et très peu d’espace. « On s’est dit qu’à chaque année, si on faisait faire une cinquantaine d’œuvres par an pour le plafond, ça serait pas long qu’on arriverait à 1000… »
Le musée a finalement laissé tomber l’objectif, lui aussi purement quantitatif, mais reste très heureux de « ce projet rigolo, où les artistes ont participé à modifier la collection », et l’espace même d’exposition.
Plusieurs de ces œuvres en hauteur ont été faites au musée même. « C’était très expérimental. Au début, certains artistes ont fait leurs dessins préliminaires au crayon, en pensant l’effacer ensuite. Mais ça ne partait pas. Regarde, ici, il en reste un… », indique Mme Lauzon en pointant un petit animal au crayon.
L’équipe a fait toute sorte de tests et abandonné la peinture phosphorescente prévue. « La meilleure, c’était la peinture fluorescente. »
En 2020, en pleine pandémie, quelques visiteurs ont ainsi pu voir cette première expo permanente du MAC LAU. « La salle était toute blanche. Il n’y avait rien à voir. Quand quelqu’un entrait, l’éclairage basculait : les lumières se fermaient, les black lights s’allumaient, la salle se révélait. »
C’est lors de cette même exposition que le musée a aussi rendu disponible une partie de sa collection, avec une réserve ouverte. Une demi-douzaine de panneaux rétractables peuvent être dévoilés par les visiteurs.
S’y retrouvent 120 œuvres — 12 % de la collection qui se consacre aux artistes des Laurentides, et qui compte des Claude Vermette, un Betty Goodwin, René Derouin, Kittie Bruneau. Autant de tableaux qui resteraient sinon inaccessibles aux yeux.

items.title: What I learned from our two summer interns: A perspective from our CEO
items.summary: Travis Bembenek reflects on mentoring two summer interns — and what their relationship with AI, reading and writing reveals about the next generation of journalists. The post What I learned from our two summer interns: A perspective from our CEO appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Part of our team’s passion for journalism extends to making sure that we do our part to help inspire the next generation of journalists. This summer, the MND team had two students working with us in our San Miguel office — Jared and Zella. The two have completely different life experiences, different personalities and different passions, so it was fun to have them both on the team.
Jared grew up in the Chicago area and is about to start his senior year at the University of Washington in Seattle. He is a journalism major and is passionate about sports journalism. Although he had been to Europe several times with his family, he had never been to Mexico. Despite having taken five years of Spanish in school, his speaking skills were quite “rusty” (to put it mildly). Jared is very much a self-proclaimed introvert.
Zella was born in Manhattan and moved to San Miguel with her family when she was six months old. She then lived in SMA until she was 15 years old, though her freshman year in high school. For the final three years of high school, she is going to a boarding school in California (her parents still live in SMA). For her upcoming senior year, Zella will be the editor-in-chief of her high school paper. She is completely bilingual and very extroverted.
As many people on our team do not have children, it presented an interesting opportunity for us to work with two kids at different phases of their “journalism journey.” At some points this summer, our office in San Miguel had team members aged 17, 21, 27, 28 and 32 (my wife’s and my ages are confidential!). The following is a list of what I learned from our two interns this summer, offered less as a verdict on them and more as a snapshot of the moment their generation is navigating.
1. Artificial intelligence presents a real dilemma for them. On one hand, they see how easy it can make their life, yet on the other hand, they also realize that it can make them overly dependent on it and lazy. It’s like the ultimate superpower, but at the same time you know it carries real risks. We made it clear to them that at MND we would allow zero AI in their writing, but that it is perfectly fine to use for research purposes.
2. Neither one of them wanted to think too much about what AI could do to the journalism profession, the news industry or their career prospects in general. It was refreshing, albeit somewhat concerning, to see them so … naive? In denial? Innocent? … about what AI could mean for them in the future. They didn’t really want to talk about it, so I didn’t push it much.
3. It’s troubling to see how few actual books they read. TikTok or Instagram videos are the new version of reading. Which, of course, is concerning. This isn’t unique to Jared and Zella — it reflects a broader shift in how information is consumed across most of their peer group.
I asked Jared when he last read a non-fiction book, to which he replied, “I don’t think I ever have read one.” So I promptly gave him two books to read: The first was “The Last Emperor of Mexico” by Edward Shawcross, a great book about Maximilian and a fascinating part of Mexican history. He loved it. The second was “Comfort Crisis” by Michael Easter, which is about the mental and physical health benefits of embracing discomfort. I have written previously about how important I think embracing discomfort is, and how important it was to me as I studied abroad years ago. I also see the benefits in it from my wife’s journey to the U.S. from India, as well as from many other immigrants. I don’t think he appreciated the book yet — these things sometimes take time to land — but I find it very unfortunate that many in society seem to be somewhat giving up on expecting kids to read books, especially non-fiction. That is not a good trend.
4. It was fascinating to see how both interns’ faces literally lit up when they were writing. For both of them, writing is clearly a “happy place.” I loved seeing that. I truly believe that writing is a wonderfu

items.title: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast: What one man’s heart surgery story reveals about healthcare in Mexico
items.summary: Co-host George Reavis shares his firsthand experience of heart surgery in Mexico — the doctors, the costs, the insurance and what he'd do differently — in the latest "Confidently Wrong" episode. The post ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast: What one man’s heart surgery story reveals about healthcare in Mexico appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
“Confidently Wrong” is back with a new episode from Mexico News Daily, and this time we are doing a deep dive into the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico. In an earlier episode, we tackled one of the most asked — and most misunderstood — topics: healthcare in Mexico. We reviewed the Expat Healthcare Survey results, digging into the responses of over 700 foreigners actively using healthcare in the country.
You can see the results of the survey here: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/mnd-intelligence/mnd-mexico-healthcare-experience-survey-1/
And you can see the episode of the podcast here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drRwz5bIuOE&list=PLejJ221QSkEk&index=4
After the usual questions about safety and life in Mexico, the conversation almost always turns to healthcare. Do you have a doctor? Is it affordable? Can you trust the system? In that episode, we broke down those questions using real data and real experiences.
The MND team surveyed foreigners living across Mexico to better understand what healthcare here is actually like. From routine dental cleanings to major procedures like heart surgery, respondents shared insights on cost, accessibility and quality of care. While no single survey can cover everything, the results offer a grounded, firsthand look at the system.
In this episode, we do a much deeper dive into the nitty-gritty of the healthcare system. We review the real-life example of George Reavis, my co-host, and his recent heart surgery in Mexico. We discuss the entire process including interactions with doctors, the procedure and health insurance. We also review what went well and what he thinks he should have done better.
I’m sure you will find, as I did, his story extremely insightful and helpful to better understand how to navigate the healthcare system in Mexico. It’s filled with unbiased, real-life anecdotes relevant to anyone wanting to learn more about the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico.
Check it out below.
Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

items.title: Mexico nets 2 Gold Medals at World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam
items.summary: Mexico's three overall medals at the Championships was a record haul for the country that included a long-sought-after Gold for star rower Kenia Lechuga for winning the lightweight race. The post Mexico nets 2 Gold Medals at World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Mexico made history at the 2026 World Rowing Championships, winning two Gold Medals and a Bronze at the event in Amsterdam.
Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez started things off Thursday with a victory in the women’s lightweight double sculls to become the first Mexican rowers to win a Gold Medal at a senior World Championships.
ESPN reported that the duo — which won gold last month at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — dominated from the outset and resisted attacks from Greece, the reigning under-23 world champion, to claim victory with a time of 7:10 minutes.
Mexico had never before won a Gold Medal at this event and its rowers had never won more than one medal at a single World Championships.
Kenia Lechuga helped turn that history around by winning the lightweight race, capturing the world title that had eluded her until now. Lechuga — Mexico’s most decorated rower — won silver in this event in 2023 and came home with a Bronze in 2025. She won gold in this event at the 2019 Pan American Games.
On Thursday, the 32-year-old Nuevo León native took the lead from the start aboard her signature pink boat and maintained control to the finish line. She completed the standard 2,000-meter course in 7:29 minutes
“We are competing fearlessly against the European monarchs,” Lechuga said afterward.
It is believed that this year’s World Championships was the last time Lechuga will compete in the lightweight category as she is expected to focus on the individual sculls leading up to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Lechuga competed in the 2016 Rio Games (finishing 12th), the 2020 Tokyo Games (finishing 16th) and participated in the open weight category at the 2024 Paris Games.
Finally, Alexis López earned a bronze medal in the men’s lightweight individual sculls, completing the 2,000-meter race in 6:52 minutes, placing him third behind Greece’s Petros Gkaidatzis and Uruguay’s Felipe Kluver. Gkaidatzis, is the reigning European champion and Kluver was world champion in 2025.
López, a native of San Felipe, Baja California, won four medals at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — two gold (individual and mixed double) and two silver (men’s double and men’s quadruple).

items.title: Editorial: Salarios: revertir el daño neoliberal
items.summary: El Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (Inegi) informó que en el primer trimestre del año los salarios representaron 30.8 por ciento del producto interno bruto (PIB), un incremento de 4.1 puntos porcentuales respecto a 2018. Sólo en los 12 meses transcurridos entre el lapso enero-marzo de 2025 al mismo periodo de este año, los salarios tuvieron un avance de 1.7 puntos porcentuales en el conjunto de la economía mexicana.
items.body_text:
l Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (Inegi) informó que en el primer trimestre del año los salarios representaron 30.8 por ciento del producto interno bruto (PIB), un incremento de 4.1 puntos porcentuales respecto a 2018. Sólo en los 12 meses transcurridos entre el lapso enero-marzo de 2025 al mismo periodo de este año, los salarios tuvieron un avance de 1.7 puntos porcentuales en el conjunto de la economía mexicana.
Esto significa que durante los ocho años recientes la distribución de la riqueza ha cambiado en beneficio de los trabajadores, lo cual también se refleja en las cifras de pobreza laboral, condición en la cual el ingreso producto del trabajo es inferior al valor de la canasta alimentaria. Este indicador se ubica en 31.9 por ciento de la población ocupada, una disminución anual de 3.2 puntos porcentuales. Si bien persisten graves rezagos en entidades como Chiapas, Oaxaca y Guerrero (con 59.8, 52.9 y 52.2 por ciento de los trabajadores en pobreza laboral, respectivamente), en otras hubo aumentos de los ingresos laborales reales de hasta 20 (estado de México y San Luis Potosí) o 30 por ciento (Morelos).
Más que simples cifras, los datos referidos dan cuenta de la transformación de la economía mexicana en los sexenios anterior y el presente. El escaso peso de los salarios en el PIB es también una medida de la desigualdad y un reflejo de decisiones políticas. Así, no es coincidencia que los países donde los ingresos de los trabajadores representan una mayor proporción de la economía sean también los que registran mayor Índice de Desarrollo Humano y los que son reconocidos por su elevada calidad de vida.
Tampoco es casual que la implantación del modelo neoliberal haya llevado esta proporción a su nivel más bajo desde que se tiene registro, como resultado, entre otros factores, de la caída en el poder de negociación de los trabajadores mediante la desindicalización y la flexibilización laboral.
Se estima que por cada punto porcentual que cae la participación de los salarios en el PIB, el Índice de Gini (la métrica estándar de desigualdad) aumenta entre 0.15 y 0.33 puntos porcentuales.
Nada está aislado. A partir de la década de 1980, el declive de la participación de los salarios en el ingreso nacional tiene su correlato en el auge de los pagos de dividendos e intereses por parte de las corporaciones no financieras. Es decir, la riqueza se desvió de las nóminas hacia los accionistas, lo cual comprueba que el neoliberalismo es, en esencia, un mecanismo para extraer capital de las clases bajas y medias y transferirlo a una minoría de ultrarricos.
En este sentido, resulta significativo que la mejoría real de las condiciones de vida de los mexicanos asalariados se logre en un periodo de bajo crecimiento del PIB, lo cual desmiente la manida falacia neoliberal de que el único camino hacia la reducción de la pobreza pasa por el crecimiento sostenido de la economía. Una vez más se comprueba que, en ausencia de políticas redistributivas, los productos del crecimiento son acaparados por quienes se encuentran en la cumbre de la pirámide económica.
El hecho de que en la actualidad México vaya a contracorriente de la maquinaria de despojo neoliberal muestra que, con sus defectos e insuficiencias, el modelo económico de la Cuarta Transformación ha convertido la bonanza de unos cuantos en bienestar para las mayorías.

Sábado 29 de agosto de 2026, p. 7
Al dar a conocer a los tres primeros finalistas del concurso binacional México Canta, la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo resaltó que el proyecto busca fortalecer el vínculo entre los jóvenes mexicanos que residen en ambas naciones.
Asimismo, promover narrativas musicales “que no tengan que ver con violencia, con drogadicción, con adicciones, sino con el amor, el desamor, el amor por la patria, con el reconocimiento de México, con historias de quienes cantan o de distintos lugares del país”, así como promover la producción musical en la nación.
La mandataria mencionó que en el país vecino hay muchos grupos mexicanos y destacó a los Tigres del Norte. “Se hicieron allá y son grupos que han ido a tocar a la Casa Blanca con distintos presidentes”.
Entonces, agregó, “a través de este concurso y de otros temas buscamos que se mantenga ese vínculo cultural familiar, porque es muy importante. La migración es difícil”.
Los finalistas del certamen, residentes en Estados Unidos, son: Tiffany Calaoiz, Joshua Soto y Rosalba Valdez. El domingo se llevará a cabo, en Mazatlán, la semifinal para los concursantes de México.

items.title: Lira, a un paso del Mónaco; Cruz Azul acuerda salida del jugador
items.summary: Erik Lira está a un paso de dar el salto al futbol europeo. Tras semanas de intensas negociaciones, Cruz Azul y el AS Mónaco han alcanzado un acuerdo para el traspaso del centrocampista mexicano por 9.2 millones de dólares (unos 8.5 millones de euros) más 3.4 millones en variables. items.body_text:
Sábado 29 de agosto de 2026, p. 9
Erik Lira está a un paso de dar el salto al futbol europeo. Tras semanas de intensas negociaciones, Cruz Azul y el AS Mónaco han alcanzado un acuerdo para el traspaso del centrocampista mexicano por 9.2 millones de dólares (unos 8.5 millones de euros) más 3.4 millones en variables. La operación incluye un contrato por cinco temporadas y la adquisición de 80 por ciento de sus derechos federativos, según fuentes consultadas en el club capitalino.
La cúpula de La Máquina mantendrá 20 por ciento restante de la carta, con la vista puesta en una futura venta. El único obstáculo para que el futbolista viaje al Principado es la gestión del cupo de extracomunitarios por parte del Mónaco, que tiene ocupadas las cuatro plazas permitidas por la Ligue 1.
El club francés debe dar salida a uno de sus extranjeros –el brasileño Vanderson, el ruso Aleksandr Golovin, el japonés Takumi Minamino o el estadunidense Folarin Balogun– antes del cierre del mercado, fijado para el próximo martes.
Según el diario L’Equipe, Balogun, seleccionado nacional del conjunto de las barras y las estrellas, ha despertado el interés de clubes como el Tottenham Hotspur y el Aston Villa. Sin embargo, ambas organizaciones incorporaron a sus plantillas elementos de características similares durante la recta final del mercado de fichajes.
Los Spurs anunciaron al atacante Omar Marmoush, mientras que los Villans llegaron a un acuerdo con el ex del Chelsea, Nicolas Jackson.
De concretarse la transacción del estadunidense o la del resto de los involucrados, el debut del internacional mexicano podría darse el próximo viernes 4 de septiembre ante el París Saint-Germain, en el Parque de los Príncipes. Entre tanto, Lira continúa acudiendo a las instalaciones de La Noria a entrenar, aunque el técnico Joel Huiqui le ha liberado de la carga de trabajo para que pueda cerrar su incorporación al conjunto francés.
“La negociación está en la recta final. Erik ha estado luchando para poder lograr el sueño y esperemos que se pueda confirmar en estos días”, declaró el miércoles el entrenador campeón del futbol mexicano.

items.title: Operativos en Sinaloa dejan 12 detenidos, 35 armas y más de 1.3 toneladas de marihuana aseguradas
items.summary: Autoridades federales y estatales realizaron operativos en Sinaloa del 20 al 26 de agosto, con aseguramientos en distintos puntos y revisiones en el penal de Aguaruto.
items.body_text:
Fuerzas federales y estatales detuvieron a 12 personas y aseguraron 35 armas de fuego, más de 7 mil cartuchos y mil 346 kilogramos de marihuana durante distintos operativos realizados en Sinaloa del 20 al 26 de agosto.
Las Comandancias de la III Región Militar y de la 9/a. Zona Militar informaron que las acciones forman parte de la Estrategia Nacional de Seguridad Pública y fueron realizadas por elementos de la Guardia Nacional y el Ejército Mexicano, en coordinación con la Armada, la Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana, la Fiscalía General de la República y la Policía Estatal Preventiva.
Como resultado de los operativos también fueron localizados e inhabilitados un campamento y un inmueble.
Aseguran armas, cartuchos y vehículos
Entre lo asegurado por el Gabinete de Seguridad se encuentran:
- 35 armas de fuego: 34 largas y una corta.
- 7 mil 549 cartuchos.
- 200 cargadores.
- 12 granadas.
- Mil 346 kilogramos de marihuana.
- 1.72 millones de pesos en efectivo.
- Cinco vehículos.
- Equipo táctico diverso.
Las autoridades señalaron que tanto las personas detenidas como los objetos asegurados fueron puestos a disposición de las autoridades correspondientes para continuar con las investigaciones y las diligencias periciales.
Guardia Nacional localiza a dos menores desaparecidos en Mazatlán
Como parte de las actividades realizadas en Sinaloa, el 21 de agosto, en el municipio de Mazatlán, personal de la Guardia Nacional localizó a dos menores de edad que contaban con ficha de búsqueda por encontrarse desaparecidos.
Los menores quedaron en calidad de presentados ante las autoridades correspondientes para continuar con los procedimientos establecidos.
Aseguran celulares y drogas en el penal de Aguaruto
En otras acciones, elementos de la Guardia Nacional, en coordinación con la Policía Estatal Preventiva, realizaron revisiones en módulos del Centro Penitenciario de ‘Aguaruto’ los días 21, 22, 25 y 26 de agosto.
Durante estas inspecciones aseguraron 20 objetos punzocortantes, seis dosis de metanfetamina y tres pipas, además de diversos dispositivos y accesorios de comunicación.
El aseguramiento incluyó:
- 23 teléfonos celulares.
- 35 cargadores para celular.
- 11 chips de telefonía móvil.
- Siete memorias USB.
- Un cable HDMI.
- 14 cables USB.
- Una banda ancha para internet.
- Un módem.
Fuerzas Armadas reportan resultados de la actual administración
La Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional informó que, durante la presente administración, el Ejército, la Fuerza Aérea y la Guardia Nacional han conseguido la detención de 51 mil 997 personas y el aseguramiento de 25 mil 941 armas de fuego.
De acuerdo con el balance presentado, también han sido asegurados 4 millones 631 mil 86 cartuchos, 116 mil 685 cargadores, 125 mil 998 kilogramos de marihuana, 48 mil 51 vehículos y mil 226 granadas.
Las autoridades señalaron que estos resultados contribuyen a debilitar las estructuras criminales y afirmaron que las acciones se realizaron con apego al Estado de derecho y respeto a los derechos humanos, con el objetivo de preservar el orden y la paz pública en Sinaloa.
